articles.title_orig: Calls grow for US death penalty halt after ‘torturous’ botched execution of Christa Pike
articles.title_zh: Calls grow for US death penalty halt after ‘torturous’ botched execution of Christa Pike
articles.content_orig:
Pike alive but in critical condition as experts call ordeal that unfolded in Tennessee ‘unimaginably barbaric’
Top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community are calling for a moratorium on the US death penalty after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Christa Pike left the prisoner alive but in critical condition and receiving life-saving medical care.
The recent spate of harrowingly botched executions across US death penalty states reached a new low late on Wednesday when Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, called off the procedure after Pike had been injected with two full syringes of pentobarbital. She is the only person to have survived being administered 5g of the sedative – a massive dose that under normal circumstances is considered fatal.
An hour after the first injection was given, she was overheard by eyewitnesses to be still breathing, choking and struggling, and was found to have a heartbeat. Her lawyers said that her current condition, and the degree to which she may have been brain-damaged through oxygen deprivation, were as yet unknown.
Sandra Babcock, a death penalty scholar at Cornell law school who advises Pike’s legal team, told the Guardian that the events that unfolded were “unimaginably barbaric. They demand accountability.”
She added that at a minimum Lee must now “commute Christa Pike’s death sentence to life imprisonment”.
Another of Pike’s lawyers, Randy Spivey, who was present in the death chamber, called Pike’s ordeal “cruel and torturous”. He said he had personally counted seven needles stuck in Pike’s left arm alone, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 killing of a teenage classmate, Colleen Slemmer. She was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Leading voices on the death penalty in America told the Guardian that the failed execution was such a violation of the constitutional prohibition on “cruel and unusual punishment” that all judicial killings had to be halted. Bryan Stevenson, an internationally renowned death penalty lawyer and founder of the Equal Justice Initiative in Montgomery, Alabama, said that many warnings had been made in recent months that US executions were flawed and unreliable.
“Nearly a dozen botched executions in recent years should have suspended executions long before now,” he said.
Stevenson said it was time to turn around the threshold question. Instead of asking whether a prisoner deserved to die for the crime committed, the question should be: “Do our governments which tolerate inequality, unreliability and bias deserve to kill?”
He added: “Last night’s tragedy makes clear we should stop the misguided policy of killing people to show that killing is wrong.”
Wednesday night was the second time in five months that Tennessee had failed to carry out an execution. In May, Tony Carruthers survived the death chamber after the execution team were unable to set up an IV line.
He has been given a new execution date for next May.
That followed Alabama, which also failed to execute two death row prisoners, Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith , having been unable to find a vein. The spectacle of prisoners being sent to their deaths, only to have the executions called off as a result of basic failures in IV procedures, has sent death penalty states scrambling to find alternatives to lethal injections.
In turn, those alternative procedures have become mired in complications and disputes. Miller and Smith were both eventually killed by Alabama using an experimental procedure, nitrogen gas, that veterinarians have banned as inhumane for the euthanasia of cats and dogs.
In June, a federal judge blocked Alabama’s use of nitrogen in executions, ruling it cruel and unusual punishment.
Other states have opted for the firing squad. But recent firing squad executions have been troubled by bullets missing the heart , to the extent that the suggestion has been raised that some of the mis-targeted shots may have been intentional.
Helen Prejean, a Catholic nun who is perhaps the best-known advocate for abolition of the death penalty in America after her book Dead Man Walking was turned into a film of the same name, told the Guardian that the events on Wednesday night were the definition of cruelty.
“This is the essence of cruelty. Take a conscious, imaginative human being, give her a date for her death, have her anticipate it over and over again, and then take her out and try and kill her. She was rendered defenceless as they deliberately attempted to kill her – what greater mental torture for a human being is there?”
Prejean added that she hoped the agony Pike had endured “would be redemptive for others, and help to wake up the nation”.
As the number of gruesome botched lethal injections rapidly mounts, the central premise that has been held up by supporters – that it is a humane, medicalised and scientific way to kill a person – has come under fire. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology in Atlanta, Georgia, who has reviewed hundreds of autopsies of executed people in the US, said that lethal injections would never deserve the label of medicine.
“This is the impersonation of a medical act. It is the theft of a medical act. So when it goes awry, that is not at all surprising to me.”
Zivot was invited to present as an expert witness at a hearing convened in August by a special master in the Pike case. He warned the senior judge that Pike had a blood condition in which her blood platelets were elevated that rendered her vulnerable to blood clots.
Zivot told the hearing that Pike, as a small woman who had been in solitary confinement on death row for almost 30 years, probably had veins that were of poor quality, small in caliber, and hard to find. “I told them. I warned them,” he said.
The special master rejected almost all the evidence presented to him.
The last time that the US saw a moratorium on executions was in 1972 when the supreme court ruled in Furman v Georgia that capital punishment was capricious and arbitrary in its rendition. The ban was lifted four years later.
Paradoxically, calls for a renewed nationwide pause are reaching fever pitch at precisely the time that pressure to carry out executions is also peaking. Donald Trump has repeatedly exhorted death penalty states and the federal Department of Justice to speed up judicial killings, and his orders are having an effect.
Last year saw the highest number of US executions – 47 across 12 states – in 16 years.
Prejean said that the answer to the growing determination of Trump and the death penalty states to carry out executions was to bring the American people closer to the action. She pointed to Gallup’s findings tracking popular sentiment towards capital punishment.
In 1993, when her book came out, 80% of Americans supported the death penalty for convicted murderers. Now that figure is 52%.
“That’s progress, though not enough. People have good hearts, but they are too removed from the process that is secret and hidden. We have got to bring this to the people, bring them into the execution chamber, so that they too become a witness.”

articles.title_orig: 2026 Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series | Race #3 | Suzuka Circuit | Preview
articles.title_zh: 2026 Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series | Race #3 | Suzuka Circuit | Preview
articles.content_orig:
October 2nd, 2026 by Justin Melillo
The Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series continues this Saturday, October 3rd, featuring 32 of the best sim racers around the globe. Next up, the competition heads to Suzuka Circuit in Japan for the third round of the five-round season.
Another two names were added to the winner’s list after Silverstone last week in Diogo Pinto and Dayne Warren. Once again, two drivers from the Red Bull / Verstappen camp and the Coanda camp, respectively, as they joined Florian Lebigre and Charlie Collins who won in the opening round. Will it be another split at Suzuka, or can one team take full control?
Live streaming of the events will begin on Saturday at 19:00 GMT (3:00 p.m. ET) via Porsche’s channels on YouTube and Twitch .
Diogo Pinto, Dayne Warren score victories at Silverstone | Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship
The biggest action from Silverstone came in qualifying and in the battle for eighth in the Sprint. Diogo Pinto just took the pole position over Alejandro Sánchez, which allowed for him to take the lead on the start and go on to win the Sprint. Behind that, Cooper Webster qualified in eighth, and was on track to finish there, but managed to pass Dayne Warren for seventh before the checkers. That wound up putting Warren in first for the Main, and Warren would go on to win after 30 minutes.
There have been seven prior seasons of the Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series, but never in those previous 64 races has there been a trip to Japan to take on the twists and turns of Suzuka International Racing Course.
One of the world’s truly great race tracks, Suzuka has been the home of the Japanese Grand Prix since the 1980s and its flowing layout regularly puts the circuit at or near the top of the list of most Formula One drivers’ favorites. As if that weren’t enough, Suzuka boats three different configurations – Suzuka East, Suzuka West and Suzuka Full, the latter two featuring a rare figure eight layout where the back straightaway crosses the front section track on an overpass.
Designed by noted circuit architect John Hugenholtz (who also designed the original Zandvoort circuit), Suzuka opened in 1962 and served primarily as a test track for Honda and as the site of sports car racing including the Suzuka 1000K and the 8 Hours of Suzuka and MotoGP motorcycle events. Suzuka was nominated to stage the Japanese Grand Prix in 1987 and has often been the site of the Formula One season finale. As such, Suzuka has been the decisive event in some of the closest battles for the World Championship of Drivers and has witnessed a number of controversial incidents, including clashes between Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost. Suzuka also hosted non-championship NASCAR races in 1996 and ’97.
In addition to its signature crossover layout, Suzuka features a number of notable challenges including a testing series of esses, the multi-apex Spoon Curve and dauntingly fast 130R corner. The race track also serves as the foundation for a major sports and entertainment facility including an amusement park whose giant Ferris Wheel is prominent in photographs and television images of the circuit.
After Suzuka, the Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship heads to the Autódromo José Carlos Pace, or Interlagos for short, for the fourth round of the season. The events are scheduled for Saturday, October 10th, and will be live starting at 19:00 GMT (3:00 p.m. ET) via Porsche’s channels on YouTube and Twitch .

articles.title_orig: Taylor T-Shirts Impact Lives Through Partnership with World Orphans
articles.title_zh: Taylor T-Shirts Impact Lives Through Partnership with World Orphans
articles.content_orig:
Lydia Wilhelm 02 October 2026
Would it really be a prospective student visit without a free t-shirt? If you see a student walking backwards across campus giving a Taylor tour, you’re bound to see some visitors with classic Taylor purple t-shirts hanging over their arms. However, you might not know that this common prospective student gift is creating uncommon change in the lives of Guatemalan families through Taylor’s partnership with World Orphans .
World Orphans is a non-profit organization with a vision of relational healing and financial independence for families who have been separated due to poverty or abuse. One of the ministry arms within the organization is the World Orphans Market , an economic empowerment program. This program equips women with sewing skills, and these women are then employed as artisans to return to them the dignity of meaningful work and financial freedom. All of World Orphans’ work is grounded in a Christ-centered philosophy of human worth: everyone is created with intrinsic dignity and with a God-given purpose. Additionally, World Orphans works through local churches, ensuring that these women are supported by Christ-centered communities as they work their way out of poverty and towards better lives for their families.
Like so many Taylor stories, Taylor’s journey to partnering with World Orphans is a story of community. When the Admissions team connected with World Orphans, they saw an opportunity—an opportunity for Taylor as an organization to model the same mission it seeks to foster in its student body. Taylor always has a need for t-shirts—particularly in Admissions. Here, Taylor’s tangible need for shirts meets these Guatemalan women’s tangible need for living-wage work, creating a true, mutually beneficial partnership.
As the Admissions team collaborated with World Orphans’ Guatemalan team, they encountered some community connections that made one thing clear—God had already been opening doors for this partnership. One of these connections was Lily Sachsenmeier ’26, who finished her Orphaned & Vulnerable Children degree interning at World Orphans in Guatemala, where "a highlight was getting to talk with social workers at World Orphans who support local families, empowering parents with education and resources to care for their children. I was really moved by the personal experiences they shared and by their passion for their work."
During her time in Guatemala, Sachsenmeier also had the opportunity to meet some of the artisans making the t-shirts for Taylor Admissions, bringing this community story full circle.
Reflecting on Taylor’s choosing World Orphans to supply their next batch of Admissions t-shirts, Sachsenmeier said, "I’m deeply touched that Taylor is partnering with World Orphans. As a student, I got many free t-shirts for events and programs, and I’m so glad that Taylor is being intentional about where they source some of these t-shirts. I’m incredibly proud that Taylor is investing in t-shirts made by these women in Guatemala as part of World Orphans’ economic empowerment program!"
At Taylor, a t-shirt is so much more than a clothing item—it’s a walking billboard for who we are. It says, "I believe in what goes on here." Now, Taylor purple has additional purpose. These t-shirts are a physical manifestation of our mission to "minister Christ’s redemptive love, grace, and truth to a world in need." They are a reminder of a God who opens doors. And a reminder of what a true partnership can look like.
Learn more about how Taylor equips students to break cycles of vulnerability through our Orphaned & Vulnerable Children major.

articles.title_orig: McMinnville siblings earn karate medals around the world
articles.title_zh: McMinnville siblings earn karate medals around the world
articles.content_orig:
MCMINNVILLE, Ore. (KPTV) - Logan and Kenzie Mendonca, a brother and sister from McMinnville, are competing in karate tournaments around the world.
“We are more stressed watching each other fight than when we are competing ourselves,” Kenzie said.
The siblings have traveled to multiple countries to compete.
“Canada, Mexico, Chile, Brazil, Paraguay, Costa Rica,” Logan said.
“I think Africa, just to make one,” Logan said, referring to places they haven’t competed.
Logan and Kenzie recently returned from Guadalajara, Mexico, with Youth League Karate gold medals. Their medals hang in the family dojo, the Mendonca Academy of Martial Arts in McMinnville.
“It’s a place of calm. I come in here and my problems are outside,” Logan said.
The siblings have competed in karate since they were three years old. Their father, Tony, leads their training routine.
“You learn time management, you learn how to get your things done because the dojo isn’t something that you can skip. It is a mandatory part of your routine,” Kenzie said.
“Just traveling and seeing crazy stuff but also winning and losing together is something really special to me,” Logan said.
Logan and Kenzie competed at the Junior Pan American Karate Championships in San Jose, Costa Rica. Logan won the Junior Male title in his fifth appearance at the event.
“I went bronze, silver, silver, then I took fifth and this year I won, so this year was my first year winning, pulling it out. It was my third year in the finals,” Logan said.
Logan is ranked No. 1 in the U.S. and is a senior at McMinnville High School. Kenzie, a sophomore, won Pan American Cadet Female silver for a third straight year.
“I think the most-cocky part of it for me is being in three finals before Logan,” Kenzie said.
“Yeah, I mean her record is better than mine,” Logan said.
“On paper if you look at like our ages my stuff looks cooler than his,” Kenzie said. “Because I’m better earlier.”
Both Logan and Kenzie were named team captains for the United States. They will next compete at the Junior World Championships in Poland.
“He’s Spiderman but when he comes home, he’s Peter Parker,” Kenzie said.
Logan is a National Merit Scholar semifinalist with aspirations of attending college in France to study physics.
“Right now Peter Parker has national merit, but nobody knows he’s Spiderman and nobody cares,” Kenzie said.
Logan and Kenzie will miss about nine days of school for the trip to Poland. They are completing tests during lunch breaks and will bring homework with them.

articles.title_orig: France student protests spread from Paris, with violent clashes forcing hundreds of high schools to close
articles.title_zh: France student protests spread from Paris, with violent clashes forcing hundreds of high schools to close
articles.content_orig:
Paris — French high school students lit fires outside schools and faced off with police on Friday as a protest movement that has forced the closure or disrupted education at more than 560 establishments showed no sign of abating.
The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils in their final years of high school block access to buildings and clash with police.
The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions inadequate including overheated classrooms and dilapidated buildings, and that there are too many staff absences.
"For a whole year, we didn't have a science teacher. We don't have any textbooks," said Simon, a 15-year-old who declined to give his surname outside the Turgot high school in central Paris. "And still, we're the lucky ones. It's even worse in the suburbs."
The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it calls "urban violence."
Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing tear gas canisters to disperse the protests.
In Paris on Friday, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools, with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said "the high school student movement is being held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups."
His ministry said Friday that education had been disrupted at more than 560 high schools out of the 3,700 in the country. More than 1,000 high schools were affected Thursday, the interior ministry has said.
Many high schools have planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille.
At least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement, Geffray told BFMTV, while about 170 students have been wounded and over 100 high schools have suffered "severe damage."
"Parents must clearly step up and tell their children not to go" to the protests, he said. "What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger."
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said he has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children during the protests and "pay for repairs."
Since the start of the movement, around 2,000 people have been taken into police custody "90% of whom were minors," Darmanin told RTL.
In the western city of Rennes, the tension was already palpable outside the Jean-Mace high school with students dressed in black and wearing balaclavas standing not far from a heavy police presence.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won — our school is closed this morning," said Lola, 16, who declined to give her last name.
She condemned what she said was police violence.
"It makes us even angrier —   the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she said.
Police used tear gas at the Kerichen high school in Brest, in western France, an AFP photographer said.
The protests have also made a strong political echo just over half a year before presidential elections, with the government accusing the hard left France Unbowed (LFI) —   whose firebrand leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is again standing for the presidency - of being behind the movement.
But senior LFI official Manuel Bompard accused the government of "descending into conspiracy theories."

articles.title_orig: Nike stock misery continues after another dreadful quarter and outlook: Wall Street reacts
articles.title_zh: Nike stock misery continues after another dreadful quarter and outlook: Wall Street reacts
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nike ( NKE ) reminded investors why the stock is trading at record lows on its earnings day.
Shares of the fallen sportswear giant dropped 6% in early trading on Friday, extending the plunge in a stock that had already dropped 76% in the past five years alone.
Nike's quarter and earnings call were littered with red flags about how far the business has fallen and how difficult the road to recovery still is:
🛑 Nike Brand sales: down 4% 🛑 Online sales: down 13% 🛑 Converse sales: down 28% 🛑 China sales: down 26% 🛑 Inventory: down only 3% 🛑 Signaled a major round of layoffs (again) 🛑 Sales seen dropping by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal year 2027 🛑 Earnings guidance well below consensus ($1.15 to $1.35 vs. estimates of $1.66)
"Overall, there's a lack of energy in the lifestyle space right now, which is impacting traffic. Yes, the consumer is cautious. But as the leader in the industry, it's on us to bring more creativity to sportswear," Nike CEO Elliott Hill said on the earnings call.
Here is the vibe on the quarter and outlook from Wall Street.
"We are not ready to call a bottom yet with shares trading at 28x P/E at the midpoint of FY27E guidance. The new Pace cost savings plan helps, and we expect it to be increased at the November investor day, helping paint a path towards a more tangible margin structure vs. the MSD% EBIT margin in FY27E. We recommend the challenger athletic footwear brands while NKE is off its game (DECK, ONON, WWW)." -Stifel analyst Peter McGoldrick
"NKE's F'1Q reinforced that the turnaround is progressing, with Performance continuing to scale while NA trends improve and profitability showing signs of stabilization. While China, Jordan, and Sportswear continue to weigh on results, mgmt's deliberate actions and revised FY27 framework suggest greater focus on rebuilding long-term brand and marketplace health." -Jefferies analyst Randy Konik
"With yet another downward revision, the questions remain when guidance cuts will represent the band-aid rip versus slow bleed as they continue to debate the path potential stabilization ahead. With the November analyst day ahead, we would assume management likely preferred to get the 'bad news' out of the way to offer up a more positive tone in person, but clearly there has been plenty of "bad news" to spare. Recognizing ongoing noise, we lower our Price Target to $50 (from $60). And though it certainly is not easy (and certainly has not been correct), we maintain our BUY rating amid increasingly negative sentiment and a potentially emerging catalyst path (potentially troughing estimates, new CFO, November Analyst Day)." -Guggenheim analyst Simeon Siegel

articles.content_orig:
Cookies allow us to understand how you use this site and improve your experience. Our detailed Cookie Policy can be found here . By continuing to use this website you accept our use of cookies.
Mandatory cookies help make this website usable by enabling basic functions like page navigation and access to secure areas of the website. Our website cannot function properly without these cookies.
Statistic cookies help us understand how visitors interact with this website, for example seeing which pages are most popular. This information is collected anonymously and helps us improve the site by making the most sought after information easy to find.
Marketing cookies are used to track visitors across websites allowing the display of ads that are relevant and engaging for the visitor. Whilst we do not display any advertising on the WJC website, allowing marketing cooking may allow other sites to see that you have visited our site.
Start time 09:00 AM (New York) / 15:00 (Brussels) / 16:00 (Jerusalem)
As we approach the third anniversary of October 7, we invite you to join the World Jewish Congress for a special online commemoration on Tuesday, October 6, with Rabbi Doron Perez , President of the World Zionist Organization and Executive Chairman of World Mizrachi.
For Rabbi Perez, October 7 is both a national tragedy and an intensely personal one. His son, Captain Daniel Perez, was killed while defending Nahal Oz on October 7, 2023, and his body was taken hostage into Gaza. For 163 days, his family held on to the hope that Daniel might still be alive. After learning of his death, they waited another year and a half until he was finally returned to Israel and laid to rest.
In this deeply personal conversation with our communities, Rabbi Perez will share Daniel’s story and his family’s journey through hope, devastating loss and remembrance. He will reflect on the faith and resilience that carried them through these unimaginable years and on the strength and hope that continue to sustain the Jewish people.
Three years after October 7, its impact continues to be deeply felt in Israel and throughout Jewish communities worldwide. This gathering is an opportunity for us to remember together, to acknowledge all that our communities have endured, and to reaffirm the connection and solidarity that bind us across borders.
We warmly invite you, your leadership and members of your community to join us and encourage you to share this invitation widely.
Registration: Webinar Registration - Zoom
We hope you will join us in remembrance, as we come together to mark the darkest day for the Jewish people since the Shoah. May the memory of those we lost forever be a blessing.

articles.title_orig: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000
articles.title_zh: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000
articles.content_orig:
The Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak has now killed more than 4,000 people, according to government data, making it the worst epidemic in the country’s history .
Figures released on Friday showed that the death toll has risen to 4,018, and confirmed cases had ⁠reached 8,300 across seven provinces, as the government continues to struggle to contain the outbreak.
Weak infrastructure, the remoteness of the region in eastern DRC, and ongoing conflict with armed groups near the borders with South Sudan, Uganda, and Rwanda have hindered efforts to respond to cases quickly and effectively.
The United Nations reported on Friday that an Ebola-hit camp housing a transit centre for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week as they were looking for weapons on the outskirts of Bunia, capital city of Ituri Province, which is at the epicentre of the outbreak.
The incident forced 19,000 people to flee the camp.
“The enormous challenge of halting the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) just became even harder after a key transit centre for patients requiring treatment burned down in Ituri province,” the UN said.
People’s mistrust and anger towards health workers and authorities have also contributed to the obstacles the government faces in its efforts to contain the outbreak.
A senior ‌member of DRC’s governing Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party was beaten to death days ago after taking part ⁠in a radio programme to raise awareness about the epidemic.
The attack on Marie-Celestin Karondwa, a local official with UDPS, took place last Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterwards, and he died at hospital from his injuries.
The World Health Organization has warned that the epidemic is “ far from over ” and on track to surpass the regional 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone.
Caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, the current epidemic became the largest and deadliest in the DRC after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.
Several treatments and vaccines are being trialled against Bundibugyo, but currently, there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
The current outbreak, which is the DRC’s 17th, has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15.
More than ⁠2,000 patients have recovered from the Ebola epidemic so far. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, although that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.

articles.title_orig: 2026 Right Livelihood laureates challenge autocracy, patriarchy, and AI bias
articles.title_zh: 2026 Right Livelihood laureates challenge autocracy, patriarchy, and AI bias
articles.content_orig:
The 2026 Right Livelihood Award is honoring women and women-led organisations confronting the world ’ s most entrenched power structures: authoritarian rule, patriarchal violence, and unchecked AI development.
Their common thread is resistance to systems that push people to the margins, and a shared insistence on putting people back at the centre.
The 2026 Right Livelihood Award, also known as the “ Alternative Nobel Prize, ” has been awarded to Jalila Haider from Pakistan “ for breaking barriers, as the first female lawyer from her Hazara community, to challenge ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution, guided by the conviction that no human being is illegal,” the Rural Women ’ s Assembly “ for organising rural women across Southern Africa into a united force defending land, seed, and bodily autonomy against corporate and patriarchal dispossession,” the Georgian Young Lawyers ’ Association “ for building and safeguarding Georgian democracy and sustaining civic power in the face of an autocratic crackdown,” and Timnit Gebru from the US “ for challenging concentrated power in artificial intelligence and pioneering digital technology rooted in justice, lived experience and human agency.”
World Council of Churches general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay commended the women honored. “ These Right Livelihood laureates exemplify the kind of empowerment that is life-flourishing, deep-rooted, and of the people,” he said, adding a special congratulations to the Rural Women ’ s Assembly from his home country of South Africa. “ I have seen firsthand the power of volunteers who can put the region ’ s food systems back into the hands of resilient people and communities.”
For over 45 years, the Right Livelihood Award has honoured and supported people leading the way to a just, peaceful, and sustainable world for all.
The 2026 awardees were chosen from 200 nominees from 72 countries. They will be honoured during a televised award presentation in Stockholm on 1 December.

articles.title_orig: Home Assistant renames Home Assistant Cloud to Link
articles.title_zh: Home Assistant renames Home Assistant Cloud to Link
articles.content_orig:
﻿Founder Paulus Schoutsen explains why the smart home platform is dropping “cloud” from its name and how a new hub and AI agents could take it mainstream.
﻿Founder Paulus Schoutsen explains why the smart home platform is dropping “cloud” from its name and how a new hub and AI agents could take it mainstream.
The open-source smart home platform Home Assistant is kicking the cloud to the curb — in name at least. “We are renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Home Assistant Link, because we hate clouds,” founder Paulus Schoutsen told The Verge in an interview ahead of today’s announcement . “Big tech ruined the cloud, so we’re out.”
The move is part of a long-term strategy Schoutsen and his team have been pursuing to make Home Assistant a mainstream smart home platform. Schoutsen says most users find the powerful platform after hitting the limits of mainstream options like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Apple Home. But it has a steep learning curve, and that’s what he’s looking to change.
I spoke with Schoutsen at the Z-Wave Summit in Boca Raton, Florida, this week about the changes and Home Assistant’s future plans, which include lowering barriers to entry by developing simpler dashboards, making setup more intuitive, and using generative AI to reduce complexity. He also said they plan to launch a new hub next year that’s more user-friendly. “We’re growing up.”
“You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.”
Renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Link is mostly symbolic. The features stay the same, aside from some back-end improvements to speed and reliability. The new name also tries to address a concern some new users had that it meant Home Assistant ran in the cloud, says Schoutsen. Home Assistant runs on local hardware and controls your smart home locally, but this means once you leave your home network, you can’t control anything.
For $6.50 a month or $65 a year, Home Assistant Link gives you a convenient way to access your Home Assistant instance from anywhere, alongside the option to enable other internet-dependent features such as integration with Alexa and Google voice control, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and encrypted backups.
The move addresses an awkward dynamic for the platform. Schoutsen and his team have spent years campaigning against proprietary cloud ecosystems, which he believes hurt the smart home, and encouraging people not to buy cloud-dependent products, all while offering a service with “cloud” in the name. However, unlike some cloud services, Home Assistant Cloud was never mandatory, and you could always replicate everything it provided with other methods; the same remains true for Link.
Schoutsen says Link is also different from many cloud services because it has no access to your data. Link is run by Nabu Casa , Home Assistant’s commercial partner, and all Link traffic is encrypted . “We can’t see it, and we don’t want to,“ he says. “You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.” The service provides a revenue stream to fund the platform’s development, with 60 percent of the profit going to the non-profit Open Home Foundation that runs Home Assistant.
For Home Assistant, cloud-dependent products are a hard no. “The cloud is ruining how people think of the smart home,” says Schoutsen, pointing to the recent examples of Nest shutting off the cloud for its early thermostats , smart TVs sending your data to the cloud without you knowing, and Weber sunsetting the June Oven’s servers . “Now you have a dumb oven that cost $1,500. It’s crazy,” he says. “People get so used to it and get so disappointed by it.”
The cloud isn’t all bad, Schoutsen concedes. Speech-to-text, backups, and AI work better online, but the problem is products that stop working without it. He wants product manufacturers to commit to offering local control by default, using open standards (Matter, Zigbee, Z-Wave, MQTT, ESPHome), never locking basic features behind a cloud, and allowing users to control their own data.
“I’d love to see a nutrition label on boxes showing if a product is cloud-dependent or not,” he says, adding that they’re building a database to help consumers find products that aren’t fully reliant on the cloud.
This stance against the cloud is likely to appeal to consumers who are increasingly concerned about who has access to their data. But Home Assistant still has a long way to go before it becomes mainstream. Schoutsen says Home Assistant is installed in an estimated 2.7 million homes, but that’s still a fraction of the reach of Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings , and Apple Home. Winning over mainstream users will be hard.
The biggest barrier to entry is complexity. Home Assistant does a lot, meaning you have a lot of choice, which can be overwhelming. “If you want to try something with Home Assistant, the answer is never no,” says Schoutsen. “We want everything to be possible, which means that the UX is more complicated, and that scares people.” In comparison, “You open Apple Home, and there’s like nothing you can do,” he says.
Over the last few years, the team has been working to remove those barriers without taking away functionality. “We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling,” he says. There are plans to launch a successor to the Home Assistant Green hub that will be easier to set up. “We want to make it more like onboarding a Philips Hue hub,” says Schoutsen.
They are also working to make the UX easier and will integrate the HACS community store — where users find and install community-built integrations — into Home Assistant next month. This should make integrations easier to find and set up. “If people haven’t tried Home Assistant in over a year, they should give it a shot,” he says.
“We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling.”
Another big push that could turn into a major selling point for the platform is a “No Device Left Behind” program . Nabu Casa is developing devices that will more easily bring people’s existing analog or legacy tech into the platform — such as old receivers, AC units, solar panel inverters, even TVs — using technology such as serial , IR, and Modbus .
Schoutsen sees AI as a big driver for Home Assistant. “AI is going to solve the complexity problem, and our biggest weakness is becoming our biggest strength,” he says. As a broad, open platform that can bring together data and controls from across your smart home, Home Assistant could provide a useful foundation for AI agents.
I used Claude to set up Home Assistant last year, and it was a big improvement over trying to figure out what on earth YAML was. “Soon you’re just going to have your agent configure your software for you,” he says. “Because people don’t want the software, they just want the solution that comes out of it.” Schoutsen acknowledges that agents raise obvious privacy concerns, but says Home Assistant keeps your data at home and you can choose which agent to trust with it, including one that runs locally.
Ultimately, Home Assistant may not need to reinvent itself to win over the mainstream if it can become the foundational layer that lets your home talk to your AI agent or platform of choice. “If you just have a box in your house that runs Home Assistant that connects all your data to your agents or to, say, Apple Home, that’s great,” he says. “That’s a win for Home Assistant.”

articles.title_orig: When teens get colorectal cancer, it’s often an aggressive form of the disease
articles.title_zh: When teens get colorectal cancer, it’s often an aggressive form of the disease
articles.content_orig:
Jo Henderson was 17 when she was diagnosed with advanced colorectal cancer . It came after months of symptoms — stomach pain, bloating, constipation — and months of testing.
“I was expecting a gluten allergy, lactose intolerance,” said Henderson, now 18, of Seekonk, Massachusetts. “Literally anything but cancer.”
Colorectal cancer in people younger than 20 is exceptionally rare: People like Henderson are about one in a million , and account for fewer than 100 cases per year in the United States. But a new study found that most cases of colorectal cancer in kids and teenagers are aggressive, and often diagnosed at advanced stages.
The findings show that “the adolescent and the youngest of the young adults are at particular risk for bad outcomes and are a unique and vulnerable population even compared to people in their 30s and 40s,” said Dr. Danielle Cameron, the director of pediatric surgical oncology at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute in Boston, who worked on the study.
“They are at higher risks for more aggressive types of colorectal cancers and more opportunities for diagnostic delays,” she said.
Cameron stressed that cases in adolescents and very young adults are “still very, very rare.” But anecdotally, experts say they are seeing rates begin to tick up.
Worldwide, rates of colorectal cancer are rising among people in their 20s and 30s. A person born in the 1990s is four times more likely to be diagnosed with colorectal cancer before age 50 than people born in the 1960s were.
Previous research has focused on colorectal cancer in adults under 50 . Cameron and her team went younger, focusing on people under 21.
The team identified 84 adolescents, with a median age of 16, in the United States who’d been diagnosed with colorectal cancer from 2012 through 2023. (Henderson was not a part of the study and Cameron was not her doctor.) The research will be presented at the American Academy of Pediatrics’ national conference in San Diego on Saturday. It has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.
Most of the young people in the study, 80%, weren’t diagnosed until their cancer had reached Stage 3 or Stage 4, which means the cancer has spread. That tracks with Henderson’s diagnosis: By the time her cancer was found, it had spread to her ovaries.
Once a cancer has spread, it’s much more difficult to treat — in the study, about 37% of the patients’ cancer returned and 45% of the patients died.
Diagnosing colorectal cancer in adolescents can be challenging. They’re decades away from colonoscopies to screen for the disease, and, according to Cameron, “the symptoms they are presenting with are vague.”
In the study, about 74% of people reported back or abdominal pain , and about 45% reported changes in bowel habits. A similar portion of people reported unexplained weight loss and about 32% had rectal bleeding.
“There are a lot more common things that cause those symptoms,” said Dr. Tara Henderson, chair of the department of pediatrics at the Yale School of Medicine, who was not involved in the research. (Tara and Jo Henderson are not related.)
Dr. Christopher Lieu, co-director of gastrointestinal medical oncology at the University of Colorado Anschutz in Aurora, Colorado, said that not every child or teenager who loses weight or has abdominal pain should get a colonoscopy, “but taking symptoms seriously is important.”
If a doctor has ruled out more common issues such as irritable bowel syndrome and things aren’t improving in the short term, doctors should consider ruling out colorectal cancer, said Lieu, who wasn’t involved with the research.
“If it is colorectal cancer, the more we can catch these cases at early stages of disease, the better outcomes will be,” he said.
And then there’s “the million-dollar question,” as Cameron calls it: What’s causing the rise in colorectal cancer in young people?
She suspects that it likely has to do with DNA changes brought on by environmental exposures during childhood.
Dr. Kimmie Ng, the director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, said that the rise in ultraprocessed food could be playing a role. Ng, who is Jo Henderson’s oncologist, noted that her previous research found that women who ate more ultraprocessed foods had a higher risk of colon polyps that can be precursors to cancer. Studies looking at whether microplastics could play a role are ongoing, she said.
A common risk factor for colorectal cancer is having a first- or second-degree relative — a parent, sibling, grandparent, aunt or uncle — who’d had the disease. But that was only the case for 20% of the people in the study.
However, “despite there being no family history, they may still have a genetic predisposition,” said Tara Henderson.
About half of the patients in the study underwent genetic testing, which revealed a handful of genetic mutations that can raise the risk of cancer. These mutations aren’t necessarily inherited; instead they can be caused by certain exposures, or simply by chance.
“It really does suggest that some of the exposures that are occurring early in life are playing a role in early-onset colorectal cancer,” Lieu said.
After her diagnosis, Jo Henderson launched into treatment. In December, she had a portion of her colon removed, as well as both of her ovaries, before undergoing five months of chemotherapy. She’s on hormone replacement medicine and will need annual colonoscopies moving forward.
A colonoscopy in August showed no signs of cancer. It was just four days before she was due to move away to college. She’s now a freshman in the Powers College of Business at Clemson University.
Kaitlin Sullivan is a contributor for NBCNews.com who has worked with NBC News Investigations. She reports on health, science and the environment and is a graduate of the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at City University of New York.
Erika Edwards is a health and medical news writer and reporter for NBC News and "TODAY."

articles.title_orig: World Trade Centers Association Establishes Global Headquarters at One World Trade Center
articles.title_zh: World Trade Centers Association Establishes Global Headquarters at One World Trade Center
articles.content_orig:
International trade organization returns to the World Trade Center site after 25 years, establishing its headquarters at a global center for business, commerce and connectivity, marking a new chapter for the Association
NEW YORK , Oct. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- World Trade Centers Association® (WTCA®) — an international trade organization connecting more than 300 World Trade Center® (WTC®) locations across nearly 100 countries and territories — today announced the relocation of its global headquarters to One World Trade Center in the Financial District of Lower Manhattan, establishing a new home for the Association at one of the world's most recognized addresses for international business and trade.
The move returns WTCA to the WTC site for the first time in 25 years and marks a significant milestone for an organization founded in New York in 1969. From its new headquarters on the 46th floor of One World Trade Center, WTCA will advance its mission of "Connecting Businesses, Globally. "
The new headquarters reflects both WTCA's longstanding roots in New York and the increasingly global nature of its work. From its new office, WTCA will continue advancing its mission to help its Members create connections across markets and facilitate opportunities for international trade and investment while creating a global gathering point for its Members, partners and business leaders.
"Returning our global headquarters to One World Trade Center is both a meaningful homecoming and a significant milestone for WTCA and our continued growth as a global organization," said John E. Drew, Chair of the WTCA Board of Directors. "New York City has been WTCA's home since our founding more than five decades ago, and today, our global network reaches nearly 100 countries and territories. This new office space gives us a dynamic setting — and a fitting global address — to bring together Members and partners from around the world as we continue building connections that support trade, investment and economic growth."
WTCA now occupies Suite 46C, a 2,556-square-foot office on the 46th floor of One World Trade Center. The built space includes private offices, a conference room, reception and pantry areas, along with an open workspace that supports day-to-day collaboration. Expansive views of the Hudson River and Midtown Manhattan provide the backdrop for the office designed to serve both WTCA's New York-based team and the Members, partners and other stakeholders who visit from across the global network.
The new headquarters also strengthens WTCA's ability to use New York as a convening point for its global Membership, showcasing the city's importance at the center of global commerce and trade. Through its network, events and programming, WTCA brings together business leaders, economic development organizations and WTC businesses to exchange market intelligence, build cross-border relationships and identify opportunities for trade and investment.
As a tenant, WTCA and its guests will also have access to Well& by Durst, a 25,000-square-foot amenity space on the 64th floor of One World Trade Center. The space includes a sky lobby, café, and 10,000 square feet of flexible meeting, conference and event space, serving as a world-class business and social hub fostering workplace creativity, collaboration, and community. Access to this premium floor expands WTCA's capacity to host gatherings and international delegations at its new global headquarters.
"The World Trade Centers Association's decision to establish its global headquarters at One World Trade Center is fitting given the organization's international reach and mission to advance trade and business connections globally. We look forward to welcoming them to One World Trade Center, an address known around the world," said Jody Durst, President of The Durst Organization.
One World Trade Center was developed by The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey and The Durst Organization in a public-private partnership.
"For more than two decades, the Port Authority has invested in rebuilding the World Trade Center as a place that drives economic growth and brings together commerce, culture and community in the heart of Lower Manhattan," said Jolene Yeats, World Trade Center Director at the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. "Welcoming the World Trade Centers Association back to the site of its original headquarters is another exciting step in fulfilling that vision – there's no place more fitting for its mission of building new bridges and creating new connections."
WTCA's office relocation comes 25 years after the Association last maintained offices on the 77th floor of the original World Trade Center's North Tower. While the return carries historical significance, the headquarters office is intended to serve a distinctly forward-looking role — providing WTCA with a permanent global base for an organization whose reach now extends across nearly 100 countries and territories. Together, the network serves as an international ecosystem for commerce, community and connection, helping businesses access new markets and supporting trade and investment across borders.

World Trade Centers Association (WTCA) is a network of more than 300 highly connected, mutually supporting businesses and organizations in nearly 100 countries and territories. As the owner of the "World Trade Center" and "WTC" trademarks, WTCA licenses exclusive rights to these brands for members to use in conjunction with their independently owned, iconic properties, facilities and trade services offerings. Through a robust portfolio of events, programming and resources that it offers its members, the goal of WTCA is to help local economies thrive by encouraging and facilitating trade and investment across the globe, creating an ecosystem built around commerce, community and connection. To learn more, visit www.wtca.org .

articles.title_orig: World Forest Week: FAO urges greater investment and action for the world's dryland forests
articles.title_zh: World Forest Week: FAO urges greater investment and action for the world's dryland forests
articles.content_orig:
FAO’s Call to Action on Dryland Forests emphasizes that proven solutions for reviving drylands already exist, and the priority is to create the conditions to implement them at scale
Dryland forests provide vital ecosystems, resources and livelihoods for communities around the world.
Rome – Forests and trees in the world's drylands sustain the livelihoods, food security and cultural identity of more than two billion people, yet they remain insufficiently recognized in global climate, biodiversity and land agendas, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
FAO’s Call to Action on Dryland Forests was launched today during a High-level dialogue on Dryland forests for food, nutrition and resilience held as part of the 10th World Forest Week, running alongside the 28th Session of the FAO Committee on Forestry (COFO) at FAO headquarters in Rome.
The call urges governments, donors and partners to strengthen the sustainable management, restoration and governance of drylands forests; better integrate them into national climate, biodiversity and land priorities; and significantly increase investment in their conservation and sustainable use. It also proposes a new Dryland Forest Support Accelerator as an enabling platform to speed up implementation, mobilize finance, and strengthen country-driven action at scale.
“Dryland forests are central to our lives, and that of future generations,” said FAO Director-General QU Dongyu in a video message. “Yet dryland forests are often underrecognized, under-monitored and under-financed. This must change.”
Drylands - which are characterized by water scarcity - host forests, woodlands and trees outside forests and cover roughly 41 percent of the Earth's land surface. They also account for 27 percent of global forest area.
Drylands produce high-demand wood and non-wood products, buffer people against drought, and provide one of the most accessible safety nets for the world's poorest households – from fuelwood and fodder to wild foods and medicinal plants. They also underpin the resilience of agrifood systems by supporting livestock, protecting soils and water resources, and providing food and income when crops fail.
But around 25 percent of dryland forest ecosystems are already degraded, driven largely by land-use change including agricultural expansion, urbanization and unsustainable resource extraction. Climate change is compounding these pressures, with longer droughts intensifying water stress and increasing fire risk. These impacts fall heavily on smallholders, Indigenous Peoples, pastoralists and local communities, as well as women and youth.
Dryland Forest Support Accelerator
The Call to Action emphasizes that proven solutions for reviving drylands already exist, and the priority is to create the conditions to implement them at scale.
At the centre of the call is the Dryland Forest Support Accelerator – an FAO-anchored, country-driven platform to help move action beyond fragmented projects. It would support countries in integrating dryland forests into national planning processes – including nationally determined contributions and land degradation neutrality targets – accessing long-term finance, strengthening monitoring, and improving coordination across sectors.
Building on FAO’s experience on drylands, notably through the GEF-7 Dryland Sustainable Landscapes Impact Program and the COFO Working Group on Dryland Forests and Agrosilvopastoral Systems, the Accelerator would organize support around three objectives:  gathering evidence and identifying country needs; supporting the implementation and scaling of proven approaches; and capturing results and lessons to inform future action.
The Call to Action further advises that governments, donors and the Rio Conventions give greater political and financial priority to dryland forests across global environmental processes, including through formal recognition of dryland forests as a priority ecosystem under the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD).

Thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries, schools set on fire in France . When the summer vacation ended and the new term started just a month ago, few could have imagined that the academic year would so quickly descend into nationwide student protests — and turmoil.
In a country beset by crises — both foreign and domestic — the eruption and rapid spread of protests by unhappy teenage high schoolers caught France off guard.
Friday brought more of the scenes that have dominated streets this week: vandalism, garbage fires, teens confronting and taunting police. Officers charging, firing tear gas and making more arrests. By early afternoon, the education ministry reported protests impacting 560 schools.
Taking grievances to France’s streets has long been a rite of passage in the country that spawned the French Revolution of 1789. To name just a few, there were the student protests in 1968, weeks of suburban unrest in 2005 and demonstrations in 2023 against pension reforms.
The students now barricading high-school gates and demonstrating with placards have shown the know-how of veterans — down to wearing masks and googles against police tear gas.
The timing of these protests — with France engaged in a presidential election race — sets them apart. Candidates campaigning to succeed President Emmanuel Macron in May have seized on the demonstations as a hot political issue.
And although constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, Macron also joined the fray, speaking out against protest violence and political manipulation of the young demonstrators.
Here is what you need to know:
The demonstrations started in the Paris region
Protests first erupted last week in the Paris region and spread nationwide like wildfire, even to smaller towns.
High schoolers are expressing broad grievances — mainly, schools are under-resourced, with dilapidated facilities and insufficient staff. Still, spending on education is one of the costliest items in the state budget that Macron's government proposed this week, with 65.5 billion euros ($74 billion) set aside for schools in the next year. That's more than the proposed 63.4 billion euros for defense.
Students also complain that school days, which often start at 8 a.m., are too exhausting and the university entrance system too complex. Some university students also joined the protests this week.
Government says it's becoming rioting, not legitimate protests
Macron's government has repeatedly said that it respects the right to peaceful protest. But it also issued written orders for police to break up protests that block access to schools and to rapidly put a stop to violence and vandalism.
Riot police have liberally used tear gas, wielded their batons and made arrests to disperse crowds.
Police and school staff have been targeted with explosive fireworks and other injury-causing projectiles. The interior ministry says acid has been hurled in some cases, and that those intent on destruction and looting have grafted themselves onto the high schoolers' movement and behaved like “criminals and vandals,” instead of “young people legitimately voicing their demands.”
Police made more than 1,900 arrests on Thursday, when 305 officers were hurt, the ministry said.
The protests and confrontations continued Friday, and unrest also spread to neighboring Belgium where about a dozen schools closed in Liege, a day after violence in the city and six arrests there.
The protests come against a backdrop of broader school concerns
There have been broader concerns in France that the schooling system is losing ground to those in other countries and failing in its mission to enable children from disadvantaged backgrounds to move up the social ladder.
Performance gaps are growing between highly advantaged and highly disadvantaged students, and overall scores in reading comprehension and mathematics have plunged, according to the latest PISA report, which evaluates students worldwide.
The government banned smartphones from high schools when the school year started in September, with officials arguing that banishing screens will improve learning. France this year also became the first country in the European Union to ban social media platforms for children under 15, but the country’s top court struck down that measure.
The protests are impacting the presidential election campaign
The unrest is sharpening political battle lines between presidential candidates.
Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has positioned himself firmly on the side of the students and has decried police actions as “savagery” and repressive. Police have been suspected of firing firing crowd-control projectiles are suspected in some of the injuries that protesters have suffered.
Mélenchon's critics are accusing his France Unbowed party of stoking violence and seeking to score political points from the protests.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen has called for broader police powers against rioters. Conservative former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, one of Le Pen's main challengers for the presidency, has condemned those who “break things, burn things, or assault people.”
Associated Press writer Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: How Real-World Registries inform oHCM Management
articles.title_zh: How Real-World Registries inform oHCM Management
articles.content_orig:
An investigator details MARVEL registry findings on AFib prevalence and ejection fraction outcomes with real-world mavacamten use.
Real-world registries offer a window into how obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM) patients treated with mavacamten fare outside the controlled setting of a clinical trial, particularly around atrial fibrillation (AFib) and ejection fraction (EF). In this segment, James MacNamara, MD, a non-invasive cardiologist and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) specialist at UVA Health, and Mariko Harper, MD, MS, FACC, director of the Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Center of Excellence at Virginia Mason Franciscan Health, discuss what the MARVEL registry showed. MacNamara turns to Harper, noting her involvement in the MARVEL registry, and asks her to describe the study's key findings. Harper explains that MARVEL evaluated 465 patients across 8 HCM and academic centers in the United States over approximately 16.5 months of real-world observational follow-up. The registry found a background AFib prevalence of about 27%, higher than earlier randomized trials or historical estimates, while new-incident AFib was notably lower, at about 2.7%. She notes these patients tended to carry high-risk profiles on AFib risk scores based on age and comorbidities, which is in line with what would be expected for new AFib incidence in this population. Harper highlights that mean EF remained preserved above 60% across the full cohort, regardless of AFib status, a reassuring finding given the field's ongoing attention to cardiac myosin inhibitor (CMI)-associated EF changes. She frames the overall takeaway as 2-fold: background AFib is common in this population independent of therapy, so screening should be routine regardless of CMI use, and most patients with AFib who are treated with a CMI do well, with preserved EF and improved symptoms. Harper adds an important caveat from the small subset of patients who experienced a transient EF drop: recurrence of AFib was disproportionately common in that group. She frames this as the clearest emerging signal from the data, that among the minority of patients who see their EF dip, AFib appears to be one of the most consistent associated variables, reinforcing the value of actively screening for arrhythmia whenever an unexplained EF change occurs.

Tip Toe refuses to be misunderstood. Premiering Oct. 2 on Starz, the British miniseries from Queer as Folk creator and Doctor Who reviver Russell T Davies set its stakes as high as the lamppost from which Alan Cumming ’s character is seen hanging, dead, just outside his home, in the very first scene. Reminders of this awful outcome open each episode, preceding flashbacks that take us through the escalation of tensions between Cumming’s Leo Struthers and his next-door neighbor, Clive Goss (David Morrissey), over the course of just 10 days. Scripty speechifying and a finale that strains believability notwithstanding, Tip Toe is, in its unabashed melodrama, a harrowing cri de coeur about masculinity in crisis and queer liberation reversed.
Leo and Clive have a few things in common. Both pushing 60, the men have been sharing a wall in outwardly identical Manchester rowhouses for 14 years. They’ve also both, when we meet them, hit rough patches in life. Clive, an electrician, is having trouble finding enough work to support a family that includes touchy 16-year-old George (Jackson Connor) and 25-year-old Saul (Joseph Evans), who assists his dad on jobs but isn’t exactly earning the kind of money that would enable him to move out. As gossip swirls that he’s cheated on her, Clive’s wife, Marie (Pooky Quesnel), constantly berates him. Meanwhile, Leo’s longtime partner, Curtis (Charlie Condou), has left him for a woman. Not only is he unmoored in his personal life, overrelying on his indulgent best friend, Stephanie (Elizabeth Berrington); he’s also struggling to manage Spit & Polish, the bar in Manchester’s gay nightlife district that he and Curtis used to run together.
Alan Cumming in Tip Toe Starz
Early one morning, Leo chases after an anonymous hookup who has just absconded with his laptop—only to find himself locked out of his house in his underwear. Clive reluctantly lets him in to call Stephanie for a spare key, making clear all the while that Leo’s lifestyle disgusts him and that he’s uncomfortable having his neighbor around his sons, one underage and the other a musclebound Adonis. The thing is, Clive’s kids are nowhere near as innocent as he thinks. And he’s drawn further out of his comfort zone when Leo, against his better judgment, hires Clive and Saul to fix some wiring at Spit & Polish. The first sign of worlds perilously colliding is when a bar employee recognizes Saul from OnlyFans . An unsubtle but rhetorically effective montage of Leo and the Gosses, each in separate rooms, indulging in their preferred forms of pornography, reveals both the secrets they’re keeping from each other and the loneliness they share.
While Tip Toe spends time with all of these characters, Leo is its protagonist. And he’s an admirably imperfect one, charming and fundamentally kind but also pugnacious, prone to exaggeration, self-centered enough to earn Stephanie’s accusation that he doesn’t really value women. (She, in turn, shows glimpses of the J.K. Rowling-style transphobia that seems to afflict British feminists more than most.) His bar functions as a portal into the lives of less privileged members of the queer and trans communities, from his old, flamboyant, gender-nonconforming friend and unrequited admirer, Melba (Paul Rhys), to a 20-something trans bartender (Iz Hesketh), who’s calling herself Zee as she deliberates on a permanent female name—and who dodges transphobic violence daily. The question of whether the visibility Leo’s generation fought so hard to win has backfired, making them all easy targets, haunts the series.
David Morrissey in Tip Toe Starz
Davies recently raged against the homophobia of the early AIDS crisis in the searing period piece It’s a Sin and looked queasily ahead to a dystopian future in the sci-fi family drama Years & Years . Tip Toe unites their themes to complete a sort of trilogy, combining the anxieties of LGBTQ people, intrafamilial alienation, economic strife, the social-media panopticon, and an overarching sense of doom into a fire sermon against our toxic present. That it shares its Manchester setting with the far breezier, Y2K-era Queer as Folk underlines just how much that community’s outlook has changed in a quarter-century. And the fact that Cumming’s phenomenal performance is airing concurrently in the U.S. with The Traitors: New Blood , which he hosts with high-camp aplomb and an androgynous glam wardrobe, highlights the cognitive dissonance of a society where queerness is embraced—by everyone except the sizable faction that actively hates it. More than just Leo’s antagonist, Clive is an avatar for straight masculinity in crisis, desperately vulnerable but too terrified of showing emotion to say so. Morrissey captures that tightness of that bind. Devalued at home and work, he dabbles in conspiracy theories and marinates in videos of “real deaths.” His story can feel like an adult Adolescence .
Tip Toe also calls to mind other recent series ( BEEF , too many reality shows about feuding neighbors) and films ( Eddington , Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri ) that translate current political and social fault lines into tête-à-tête conflicts. On both sides of the Atlantic, storytellers are trying to understand the hateful tenor of the contemporary public sphere by distilling it down to its simplest, me-against-you form. The difference here is that, although Leo and other characters are shown to have healthy senses of humor, Tip Toe itself doesn’t share those titles’ tone of black-comic absurdity. It isn’t a funny show. Sometimes its seriousness veers into stridency. I didn’t find the abrupt escalation to Leo’s death particularly convincing.
Yet, as in It’s a Sin and Years & Years , it’s the incandescent clarity of Davies’ anger and fear that make Tip Toe powerful. For all the dumbed-down dialogue we get from streamers worried they’ll lose distracted viewers unless someone on screen recaps the plot every five minutes, it’s rare to hear characters plainly state things like: “History tells us one thing—that blood and fire and retribution always happen. And right now it’s coming for us.” When Stephanie confesses her worry that she’ll die in 30 years without living to see the pendulum of progress swing society out of what she calls a “new Dark Age,” I suspect she’s speaking for a lot of people. Too often in fiction (which this is, despite ending title cards that purport to update us on the characters’ lives post-Leo), social commentary is inoculated with optimism or couched in irony. In its unblinking earnestness, Tip Toe ’s melodrama accesses a truth that transcends any shortcomings of its plot.

articles.title_orig: New Preliminary Real-World VEOZAH™ (fezolinetant) Data Highlights Improvements in Menopause-Related Symptoms and Sleep Outcomes
articles.title_zh: New Preliminary Real-World VEOZAH™ (fezolinetant) Data Highlights Improvements in Menopause-Related Symptoms and Sleep Outcomes
articles.content_orig:
NORTHBROOK, Ill. , Oct 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Astellas Pharma U.S., Inc. (Head of US Commercial: Mike Petroutsas, "Astellas") presented a new preliminary analysis from the Phase 4 OPTION-VMS real-world study of non-hormonal therapies (non-HTs) for bothersome vasomotor symptoms (VMS, also known as hot flashes and night sweats) at the 2026 International Menopause Society (IMS) 20 th World Congress on Menopause. The analysis showed that VEOZAH (fezolinetant 45mg) treatment was associated with statistically significant improvements from baseline in bothersome VMS at week 12, the study's primary endpoint, and improvements were observed as early as week 4. 1 VEOZAH is approved in the U.S. for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.
Statistically significant improvements were also seen across patient-reported† and objective (obtained with a medical grade wearable) sleep measures for the first time at weeks 4, 8 and 12, including a mean reduction of 2.6 nighttime awakenings from baseline at week 12. 1
Sleep disturbances are among the most commonly reported and bothersome symptoms during menopause, affecting an estimated 40–60% of menopausal women. Women with moderate to severe hot flashes are almost three times more likely to report frequent nighttime awakenings compared with women without hot flashes. 2
OPTION-VMS is a Phase 4 real-world study of women prescribed non-hormonal therapies (fezolinetant, SSRIs/SNRIs* and other non-HTs e.g. gabapentin, oxybutynin) for bothersome VMS and other menopause-associated symptoms in routine clinical practice. 1 By combining women's reported sleep experiences with objective, wearable-derived actigraphy sleep data, OPTION-VMS provides new preliminary real-world insights into sleep outcomes in routine clinical practice. The study was not designed to assess differences between treatment groups.
The preliminary analysis found that women treated with fezolinetant experienced statistically significant improvements from baseline in:
No new safety signals were seen with fezolinetant. Hepatic laboratory findings were mild and infrequent (2 cases of non-serious mildly elevated liver tests), none of which led to treatment or study discontinuation. 1
Prof. Marla Shapiro, C.M., Department of Family and Community Medicine, University of Toronto, Canada, and lead author of the OPTION-VMS oral presentation , commented: "Hot flashes and night sweats can have a far-reaching impact on women's daily lives, including their sleep, quality of life and overall well-being. These preliminary real-world findings add to the growing body of evidence from OPTION-VMS, demonstrating improvements in bothersome vasomotor symptoms and sleep outcomes among women treated with fezolinetant. Taken together with the broader study findings, these data contribute to a more complete understanding of women's experiences in routine clinical practice and may help inform discussions between women and their healthcare providers."
These preliminary real-world findings reinforce data from the VEOZAH clinical trial program and are complemented by interim data from the ongoing GRACE real-world study in Germany and the ongoing ADELE-AU, real world study in Australia, also being presented at the International Menopause Society (IMS) 2026. 3,4
Additional data presented at IMS 2026 provide supporting pre-clinical, clinical and real-world evidence across different study settings and geographies. 5,6,7,8,9
Shayna Mancuso, D.O., FACOG, Executive Medical Director and Head, U.S. Medical Affairs, Women's Health, Astellas "These preliminary real-world findings provide valuable insights into outcomes observed with fezolinetant (VEOZAH), including sleep quality, among women experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes and night sweats. By evaluating women's experiences in routine clinical practice, we are building a deeper understanding of the outcomes that matter most to women and their clinicians."
Fezolinetant is a non-hormonal, selective neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist specifically designed to block neurokinin B binding on kisspeptin/neurokinin/dynorphin neurons, which are involved in regulating the brain's temperature control center. By targeting this pathway, fezolinetant helps reduce the frequency and severity of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause. 10,11 It is currently approved in 50 countries.
† Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Sleep Disturbance – Short Form 8b
* Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)/Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs)
About OPTION-VMS OPTION-VMS (NCT06049797) is a Phase IV, longitudinal, observational, study of women aged 40-75 years with confirmed menopausal hot flashes and night sweats (also known as vasomotor symptoms or VMS) who were prescribed a non-hormonal therapy for the treatment of bothersome hot flashes and nights sweats by their healthcare provider in a real-world setting. 1 The primary objective of the study was to check if the hot flashes and night sweats that bother women change after 12 weeks (3 months) of treatment from baseline; additional outcomes include sleep quality, menopause-related quality of life, sexual health, mood, work productivity and safety.
About ADELE ADELE is an ongoing real-world observational study of women in Australia over the age of 40 who are being treated with fezolinetant for moderate to severe hot flashes and night sweats, with sleep disturbances. 4 The primary objective of the study is to evaluate improvements in real-world sleep disturbances after 12 weeks of treatment. Additional objectives include better understanding of treatment satisfaction and adherence, and treatment impacts on menopause-related quality of life (QoL) and adverse events.
About GRACE GRACE (NCT07455812) is an ongoing 24-week real-world observational study of women in Germany who have menopausal hot flashes and night sweats and have been prescribed fezolinetant. 3 The primary goal of this study is to learn about the effectiveness and safety of fezolinetant through patient surveys conducted before participants' first dose, assessed through validated patient-reported measures, including symptom improvement, menopause-related quality of life, sleep disturbance, treatment satisfaction and safety, with follow-up surveys taking place 1 week, 12 weeks and 24 weeks after their first dose.
About VEOZAH TM (fezolinetant 45 mg) VEOZAH (fezolinetant 45 mg) is a selective neurokinin 3 receptor (NK3R) antagonist, currently approved in 50 countries for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause. Fezolinetant works by blocking neurokinin B (NKB) binding on the kisspeptin/neurokinin/dynorphin (KNDy) neuron, to modulate neuronal activity in the brain's temperature control center helping restore the balance in the brain's temperature control center (the hypothalamus) to reduce the number and intensity of hot flashes and night sweats due to menopause. 10,11
About Astellas Astellas is a global life sciences company committed to turning innovative science into VALUE for patients. We provide transformative therapies in disease areas that include oncology, ophthalmology, urology, immunology, and women's health. Through our research and development programs, we are pioneering new healthcare solutions for diseases with high unmet medical needs. Learn more at www.astellas.com .
