articles.title_orig: The 1893 World's Fair Is the Subject of a New 'Chicago Stories' Documentary
articles.title_zh: The 1893 World's Fair Is the Subject of a New 'Chicago Stories' Documentary
articles.content_orig:
“This fair not only changed Chicago, it shaped the American imagination,” says Peter Marks, one of the producers and writers of the new documentary The World’s Fair of 1893 , which leads off a new season of our Chicago Stories on Friday, October 2 at 8:00 pm and at wttw.com/chicagostories . Walt Disney’s father was a carpenter who helped build the fair, while the illustrations of the Emerald City in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum, who attended, look “an awful lot like the White City” of the fair. The World’s Columbian Exposition not only inspired people; it also showed the world a new Chicago and introduced Vienna Beef, the zipper, and much more.
We spoke to Marks, his fellow producer and writer Tania Lindsay, and digital producer Meredith Francis about the fair, the documentary, and the companion website.
The Guide: Why is this World’s Fair so important to Chicago?
Peter Marks: This is the moment Chicago announced itself to the world. Only 20 years after the Great Fire , Chicago had transformed into an economic powerhouse and the birthplace of the skyscraper. [The skyscraper is the subject of another new Chicago Stories .] But people, especially New Yorkers, still dismissed us as a smelly ‘cow town.’ When Chicago beat out New York for the right to host the World’s Fair, Daniel Burnham and John Root had less than three years to turn a swamp in Jackson Park into a city that would dazzle and delight the world. Twenty-seven million visitors later, nobody could call Chicago a cow town anymore.
Tania Lindsay: It put the city on the map as a rival to New York and Paris. It also physically reshaped the city and seeded institutions, ideas, and products we still use daily.
The Guide: Why revisit the World’s Fair now?
Lindsay: Partly because there is no bad time to revisit the wonder that was the White City. And partly to remind Chicago of something about itself: That this is a city with a long history of doing hard and wonderful things, if imperfectly, and showing the world that we are much more than whatever the news says in any given year. The imperfect part matters too, and while we celebrate all the glorious wonders of the fair, the film doesn’t skip the hard parts, like who got left out, who got taken advantage of – or worse – and who carried on despite tragedy.
Marks: I think there’s something valuable about remembering a moment when Chicago took on the impossible. The fair is a reminder of Chicago’s “I Will” spirit, and what we can accomplish when we think big.
The Guide: How did you try to take a new approach towards a topic many Chicagoans already know?
Marks: One of the things we wanted to do was separate H.H. Holmes the murderer from H.H. Holmes the myth. Many people have read The Devil in the White City , in which Holmes builds this elaborate murder castle to lure unsuspecting victims. But that isn’t quite what happened. Newspaper reporters exaggerated the details, publishing fabricated diagrams of secret chambers and a crematory.
Meredith Francis: Another darker story to come out of the fair was the assassination of Chicago's mayor, Carter Harrison, just a couple days before the fair was set to close.
The Guide: What is something new that you learned in making this documentary?
Lindsay: Brownies can be highly controversial. While Bertha Palmer’s kitchen at the Palmer House Hotel is given credit as inventor of the beloved brownie, others question whether that apricot-glazed confection should be considered a brownie at all. It’s a highly sensitive topic. Some historians refused to comment, others cautiously avoided picking a side. Some said one thing off the record, and something different on. We may never know the right answer. But we’ll always have brownies.
The Guide: What’s something that most Chicagoans don’t know about the fair?
Marks: Most Chicagoans think the World’s Fair vanished, but it didn’t. If you walk down the Midway Plaisance at the University of Chicago, that’s where belly dancers once strutted and the first Ferris wheel spun. The Museum of Science and Industry was originally the Palace of Fine Arts. The Art Institute was created for the fair. There’s a ticket booth tucked in the yard of a private residence. The Obama Presidential Library rises on ground where the Horticulture and Women’s Building once stood. The fair is still very much around us if you know where to look.
Francis: On the companion website, we want people to be able to immerse themselves in this world, and to be able to imagine what it might have been like to attend the fair. We have some amazing historical images that go beyond the typical picture people might have in their heads. Our talented graphics team has created a really cool 3D imagining of what it would have been like to walk through the fair. It gives you a sense of just how expansive it was, and what it took to achieve that.
The Guide: What’s your favorite lasting impact of the fair?
Marks: For me, it’s Daniel Burnham’s vision. The White City helped inspire the City Beautiful movement and Burnham’s 1909 Plan of Chicago . There are times our skyline, parks, and museums still take my breath away.
Francis: There are a couple things that I would argue have made my life better: An early model of the modern dishwasher (invented by a woman!), and the brownie.
Lindsay: My favorite may well be the Ferris Wheel. I love that it exists because Chicago had a serious case of envy and wanted to top Paris’s 1889 World’s Fair stunner, the Eiffel Tower. George Ferris engineered the first-of-its-kind, giant wheel, with riding cars the size of city buses. It was a sensation when it debuted on the Midway Plaisance, which helped become the blueprint for the modern amusement park . Every time I see the wheel at Navy Pier, I see part of the Fair’s legacy, still spinning today.

articles.title_orig: Concerns About ‘WWII Allies’ at US-China Summit - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: Concerns About ‘WWII Allies’ at US-China Summit - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
At the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, both leaders spoke of the fact that the United States and China had been allies in World War II and had fought together. Of course, the United States and China (the Republic of China) were indeed Allied nations in WWII and fought together against Japan and others, and if the summit remarks were intended simply to reaffirm that historical fact and invoke shared memory, then they should give rise to no particular concern.
It is also worth recalling that in 2015, the 70th anniversary of the end of the war, U.S.-China relations were relatively stable, and China was emphasizing that it had fought alongside the United States and other major Western powers as key members of the Allied coalition, and had jointly created the postwar order. At that time, China was using the phrase “New Model of Major-Country Relations” in its relations with the United States. If the invocation of wartime partnership at the recent summit was intended to evoke memories of that 2015 period and signal an intention to restore the “New Model of Major-Country Relations,” that too would be comprehensible as a matter of Chinese policy.
However, more than ten years have now passed since 2015, and China’s narrative on history today is different from what it once was. So the fact that wartime partnership was raised by both sides at this summit is, in fact, a cause for concern. To explain, it is necessary to look at how China has recently been employing its historical narrative — with particular attention to its relationship with Russia.
The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 and China’s response to it, together with Russia’s war in Ukraine beginning in 2022, generated widespread international criticism of both countries. That criticism brought China and Russia closer together, and the two countries more openly positioned themselves in opposition to Western nations. In 2024, the 75th anniversary of the establishment of Sino-Russian diplomatic relations and a year in which the pandemic was still fresh in mind and the war in Ukraine was very much ongoing, Russian President Vladimir Putin made an official visit to China in May and issued a joint statement. It included the following passage:
“China and Russia will continue to firmly defend the results of the victory of the Second World War and the postwar world order enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations, and oppose the negation, distortion, and falsification of the history of World War II. They plan to solemnly celebrate the 80th anniversary of the victory of the Chinese People’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Soviet Union’s Patriotic War in 2025 and jointly promote a correct view of the history of World War II.”
This statement signaled that China and Russia intended to jointly insist on what they view as the “correct history” of WWII to the world, while refusing to accept any historical perspective that differs from their own.
In March 2025, at a press conference on the occasion of China’s National People’s Congress, State Councilor Wang Yi stated that, marking the 80th anniversary of victory in WWII, China and Russia were reaffirming that they had fought together in Asia and Europe at the cost of blood, and went on to say that, building on this past, the two countries would jointly promote a correct understanding of WWII history, defend the fruits of that victory, uphold the international system with the United Nations at its core, and advance the international order in a more just and reasonable direction. China and Russia have thus pledged not only to reaffirm their wartime partnership but to jointly seek to shape the present international order on that basis. For China and Russia, historical narrative is inseparable from the shaping of the current international order.
Then, on May 9, 2025, Russia’s Victory Day commemorating the defeat of Nazi Germany, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Russia and issued a joint statement with the Russian president. This statement explicitly identified Japanese militarism and Nazi Germany as the adversaries China and Russia fought in WWII, and made clear that China and Russia would together resist any moves to revive the militarism or Nazism of the past. On Japan specifically, the statement declared that “the Japanese government should learn lessons from the brutal crimes it committed in history, exercise caution in its words and deeds on historical issues such as the Yasukuni Shrine, and completely cut ties with militarism that once brought deep disasters to the peoples of the world and Japan itself.”
In its discourse on WWII, China was not only seeking to spread what it calls the “correct historical perspective” together with Russia, but was also issuing strong warnings against “Japanese militarism.” And this was positioned not merely as a matter of the past but — particularly in the context of the Sino-Russian relationship — as something linked to joint efforts toward a “just” reshaping of the international order.
In 2025, China made a qualitative leap in its narrative on history, in both substance and in method. China generated narratives connected to the invalidity of the San Francisco Peace Treaty, the Taiwan issue, and the status of Okinawa — areas directly linked to China’s interests in the First Island Chain. Yet China’s actions were moving faster than its words; its military activity had already extended well beyond the First Island Chain, expanding into the Second Island Chain, the Western Pacific, and the South Pacific.
From around the time of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s remarks in November 2025 and into 2026, China’s verbal attacks on Japan began to employ the term “neo-militarism,” and its criticism of Japan became more comprehensive. Japan’s security policy as a whole began to be characterized and challenged as “neo-militarism.”
In May 2026, when Putin made another official visit to China and a Sino-Russian joint statement was issued, language criticizing Japan’s “neo-militarism” and “remilitarization” was incorporated into the text, which represented an expansion of Sino-Russian historical cooperation on WWII. China also sought to extend its criticism of Japan to countries beyond Russia, inserting language critical of Japan — such as opposition to “militarism” — into joint statements issued in the context of bilateral relationships with various countries. At the UN General Assembly in September 2026 as well, the Chinese representative strongly criticized Japan using terms such as “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov joined in, expressing agreement with the Chinese position by similarly characterizing Japan as following a path of militarism.
Which brings us to the recent U.S.-China summit, where Xi and U.S. President Donald Trump raised the subject of the wartime relationship between the United States and China in WWII. The United States and China were Allied nations in WWII. But in light of the account above, China’s recent discourse on WWII is certainly not limited to pointing out historical facts or evoking memories of the past. And for Japan, that is cause for concern.

articles.title_orig: Exynos 2700 Enters Mass Production, Claims Tipster, 10% Higher Volume Than Exynos 2600 & 10% Higher Multi-Core Performance Than Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
articles.title_zh: Exynos 2700 Enters Mass Production, Claims Tipster, 10% Higher Volume Than Exynos 2600 & 10% Higher Multi-Core Performance Than Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
articles.content_orig:
There’s positive news about the final 2nm smartphone chipset that’s scheduled to launch this year from Samsung. Based on the latest rumor, the Exynos 2700 has apparently entered mass production, with the Korean giant ramping up the initial volume of its SoC by 10 percent compared to the Exynos 2600 . Also, at least according to internal tests, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is slower.
Samsung may not have made the official announcement concerning the Exynos 2700, but Ice Universe may have a ton of people with their ear to the ground because he states that the company’s next-generation 2nm silicon has entered mass production. With the Exynos 2600 fabricated on Samsung’s SF2 node, the Exynos 2700 will go one step beyond and utilize the SF2P process, ensuring slightly better performance and efficiency.
So far, Exynos 2700 appears to be 9.5 percent faster than the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 in Geekbench 6’s multi-core benchmark, possibly thanks to a new 4.00GHz target frequency . However, Samsung’s internal tests don’t mention any details of power draw or any other useful metrics, so we’ll have to treat this data with a pinch of salt for now. As for whether the company has sufficient confidence that it’ll incorporate the Exynos 2700 into the upcoming Galaxy S27 Ultra, nothing has been confirmed for now.
🔥 BREAKING: Samsung has officially begun mass production of the Exynos 2700, and this chip could be far more important than expected. Key details: • Exynos 2700 has entered front-end wafer mass production, moving beyond the small-scale sample stage. • Production volume is…
From the looks of it, Galaxy S27 models sold in the U.S. and China will be treated to Qualcomm’s SoCs, but Samsung’s MX Division is rumored to be evaluating performance, thermals, cost, and SF2P production capacity in an effort to conclude whether increasing Exynos 2700 production is economically viable. After all, proceeding to use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 is also a costly move, given that these chipsets are manufactured on TSMC’s 2nm “N2P” technology.
Samsung typically unveils its new SoCs right before the new year starts, so expect an Exynos 2700 press release to grace us in the month of December or possibly before that.
About the author : Omar Sohail is a reporter and analyst for Wccftech's mobile section, specializing in the technology and business of the mobile industry. His expertise lies in the intricate hardware supply chain, covering developments in semiconductor manufacturing, chip lithography, and camera sensor technology.
Follow Wccftech on Google to get more of our news coverage in your feeds.

articles.title_orig: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
articles.title_zh: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
articles.content_orig:
Subscribe to our newsletter
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.
China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.
Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.
Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.
China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.
Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.
According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.
“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.
South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.
Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.
China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

articles.title_orig: Josh Jolly and Sienna Pal land on World Cup podium in China
articles.title_zh: Josh Jolly and Sienna Pal land on World Cup podium in China
articles.content_orig:
Home → ← News → Josh Jolly and Sienna Pal land on World Cup podium in China
The ARA Australian Cycling Team has finished Round 5 of the 2026 UCI BMX Racing World Cup with two bronze medals, won by Josh Jolly and Sienna Pal.
Jolly showed why his highly anticipated elite debut was worth the wait as he battled through the pack from a sixth place start to finish third in Mentougou, China.
The current under-23 world champion and former junior world champion slotted in seamlessly among the heavy hitters throughout the day after winning his first round moto.
A post shared by ARA Australian Cycling Team (@auscyclingteam)
The 20-year-old said reaching the podium in his first elite appearance was "awesome".
"I had high expectations of myself coming into the elite class and I’m happy that I proved to myself that I'm good enough and my expectations were correct," Jolly said.
"⁠I’ve been waiting for the day I move to elite on the World Cup series. I’ve just been trying not to make a big deal of it, so I don’t worry myself about being with the fastest guys in the world, and I've proved to myself that I'm one of the fastest in the world now too.
"In the final, I knew I had the speed around the track to pass anyone I needed too so I was confident in making moves."
Jolly's brilliant result was followed by a determined Pal scoring her second elite World Cup podium.
The 21-year-old dived down the inside of Switzerland's Zoé Claessens in the second corner and held the Olympic bronze medallist at bay down the third and fourth straights.
Only 0.036 seconds separated Pal and Claessens at the finish line, but it was enough for the Australian to clinch third behind Laura Smulders (Netherlands) and world champion Bethany Shriever (Great Britain).
A post shared by ARA Australian Cycling Team (@auscyclingteam)
"I feel so stoked. I was already happy and enjoying myself before finishing on the podium. This third is just a cherry on top and only good information to just keep doing what I’m doing," Pal said.
"In the final, I chose gate eight to just execute my process with less interruption. I felt most comfortable there so the plan was to execute and after that first jump just get to the inside as fast as I can.
"The last two years have been a bit of a rollercoaster since last being on the podium in 2024.
"Initially, I realised the potential but then started feeling the pressure. I’ve changed a lot with all my experiences since then, now knowing I belong here at the top level of this sport and keep that smile, follow your process and the good blessings will come when they come.
"Today was one of those good blessing days!"
Jesse Asmus narrowly missed the podium in his first outing sporting the world champion rainbow jersey, finishing fourth behind Jolly.
For Teya Rufus, a touch of wheels in the first corner of her quarterfinal that nearly brought the 20-year-old down ended her day despite a late charge back to fifth.
Round 6 of the UCI BMX Racing World Cup season will be raced tomorrow.

articles.title_orig: U.S., China buy more time to iron out trade wrinkles
articles.title_zh: U.S., China buy more time to iron out trade wrinkles
articles.content_orig:
When President Donald Trump recently hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping, there were expectations in farm country that some type of major deal would be announced to boost agricultural exports. Now, farm groups are analyzing the details and trying to figure out the timeline.
The White House released a list of goods due to receive reciprocal tariff reductions under a previously announced United States-China board of framework, which would affect $30 billion in goods from both the U.S. and another $30 billion from China. Potentially the deal could boost market access for U.S. farm products and improve access to the U.S. market for everything from Chinese toys and fishing tackle.
The deal essentially drops the country-specific levies on those products on the list, returning most to “most-favored-nation” status levels.
Dubbed the “30-for-30” framework, the announcement comes as the White House is seeking to forge stronger relations with Beijing after a tense trade war at the start of Trump’s second term.
“From agricultural products to medical devices, President Trump is unlocking improved market access for about 30% of U.S. exports to China, while benefiting consumers with imports from China of household goods, toys, and other products that the United States generally does not import from other countries,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a press release.
While the list includes U.S. wheat and corn, it notably did not include whole soybeans, which are still subject to a 10% tariff.
The American Soybean Association said it’s disappointed that soybeans were excluded from the list of products getting a lower tariff.
“China’s remaining 10% retaliatory duty limits access for private Chinese importers, meaning soybean trade will continue to be handled primarily by China’s state-owned enterprises. Removing the tariff would improve the competitiveness of U.S. soybeans and provide greater opportunity for private Chinese buyers,” ASA noted.
At the same time, ASA pointed to China’s continued commitment to purchase a minimum of 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans annually in years 2026, 2027 and 2028. These annual commitments provide important demand and greater certainty for U.S. soybean farmers.
“As soybean farmers look to strengthen and expand markets, China’s annual commitment to purchase 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans provides critical stability, and we expect those commitments to be fully met,” said ASA President and Ohio soybean farmer Scott Metzger. “China remains an important market for U.S. soybeans, and we want to see a strong trading relationship that allows more customers in China to purchase our soybeans.”
Soybeans weren’t completely left out of the agreement. The list identifies soybean seeds, soybean flour, soybean oil and its separated products, soybean cake and soybean residues, as in line for tariff cuts.
China is a big market for soybeans. The U.S. used to dominate the Chinese soybean market, but after the trade war during the first Trump administration, China turned to Brazil to fill that space.
Between October 2017 to March 2018, the U.S. exported 24.43 million metric tons of soybeans to China, according to USDA’s Economic Research Service . During that same time period in 2018-2019, Chinese imports of U.S. soybeans fell to 2.69 MMT. Brazil on the other hand, saw its market share grow by 11.47 MMT, increasing exports from 14.23 MMT. to 25.70 MMT.
The U.S. has struggled to regain that market. The Trump administration on Nov. 1, 2025, unveiled a deal in which China agreed to purchase at least 12 MMT of U.S. soybeans during the last two months of 2025 and at least 25 MMT of U.S. soybeans annually from 2026 through 2028. China has purchased roughly 12 MMT of soybeans since October 2025.
The list of U.S. goods to enter China outlined 1,619 items, many of which are agricultural goods, including livestock like cattle, goats, pigs, turkey, and chicken. It also opens the market to U.S. ranchers seeking to sell beef and pork products, or other meat items. The list also names fruits and vegetables such as broccoli, sweet corn, potatoes, bananas, and citrus fruits.
The framework will also open the market for U.S. dairy. It outlines food products made from malt extract, grain flour and dairy products, in addition to items such as milk, yogurt and whey.
The U.S. Dairy Export Council described the two-month extension of the tariff truce as a “welcome step forward.”
“We are encouraged by the inclusion of U.S. dairy exports on the list of products to be considered for tariff reduction,” said Krysta Harden, president and CEO, U.S. Dairy Export Council. “USDEC urges the Board to swiftly deliver the full elimination of the retaliatory tariffs that still weigh on U.S. dairy so our suppliers can compete on a more level playing field.
The export council also cautioned the administration on port fees.
“As wider talks continue, it is essential that proposed port fees on Chinese ships are not passed along to U.S. agricultural exporters. Added freight costs would undercut the very gains the Board of Trade is meant to achieve,” Harden added.
The deputies to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Greer and Chinese Vice Premier of the State Council He Lifeng will monitor the bilateral trade of the products covered by the framework and can make adjustment proposals; however, the two countries don’t imagine making adjustments more often than on an annual basis.

articles.title_orig: Broadcom Starts Amassing $60 Billion to Fund Chips for Anthropic
articles.title_zh: Broadcom Starts Amassing $60 Billion to Fund Chips for Anthropic
articles.content_orig:
Banks are set to syndicate a $42 billion senior-secured tranche, while Blackstone is leading an $18 billion junior debt tranche
Broadcom $AVGO is assembling $60 billion in debt financing to help Anthropic and other companies access AI chips and infrastructure, according to Bloomberg . For the deal, banks are readying syndication letters covering a $42 billion Class A senior-secured tranche, while Blackstone leads an $18 billion Class B junior debt tranche—putting up $9 billion of its own capital and planning to syndicate the rest, according to Bloomberg.
A representative for Broadcom declined to comment.
The deal has been in development for weeks and has drawn close attention from investors and dealmakers in both Wall Street and Silicon Valley, according to Bloomberg. The deal is seen as a gauge of continued appetite for funding AI infrastructure buildout at a time of public pushback against data-center construction.
The arrangement fits into a broader pattern of chip companies using their financial positions to drive hardware demand. Anthropic's IPO prospectus, which revealed the terms of Broadcom 's lending commitment to the AI company , showed that Broadcom has agreed to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion to help cover infrastructure spending. That amount would cover approximately one-third of the $125.2 billion Anthropic has committed under a five-year lease for tensor processing unit computing capacity, according to CNBC . The notes could be converted into Anthropic equity, and Broadcom has the option to bring in a financing partner under the terms of the deal, according to CNBC.
Anthropic is expected to become Broadcom 's largest compute customer in 2027, according to CNBC. Broadcom and Google $GOOGL have collaborated on multiple generations of TPU chips, and Anthropic announced in April an expanded agreement with Broadcom and Google for roughly 3.5 gigawatts of computing capacity built on Google 's TPUs, with that capacity expected to come online starting in 2027.
In its prospectus, Anthropic flagged that Broadcom 's dual position as a chip supplier and lender gives rise to "potential conflicts of interest" that could compromise Anthropic's access to the computing resources it needs, according to CNBC. The prospectus also noted that decisions Broadcom makes on pricing and equipment availability could undermine Anthropic's ability to build out its infrastructure, and that triggering certain payment or performance defaults could accelerate a material portion of its lease obligations while cutting off access to the $42 billion credit line.
The $60 billion package adds to hundreds of billions of dollars in debt already raised to build out AI infrastructure, according to Bloomberg.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s China Reset: From strategic competition to transactional coexistence
articles.title_zh: Trump’s China Reset: From strategic competition to transactional coexistence
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump’s China policy has undergone a significant recalibration between his first and second terms. The first Trump administration marked a decisive break with the assumptions of engagement, moving Washington towards a broad conception of “strategic competition” that encompassed trade, technology, ideology, human rights, Taiwan and the wider military balance. The second term, by contrast, has retained the coercive instruments of the earlier approach but narrowed their purpose, increasingly subordinating them to transactional economic bargaining. Chinese President Xi Jinping’s recent visit to Washington captured this evolution: considerable ceremony and leader-level theatre, but limited substantive movement on the structural disputes defining the relationship.
Trump’s first term represented a fundamental shift in the US approach to China. Washington increasingly treated Beijing not as a prospective stakeholder in an American-led order, but as an economic and strategic challenger whose rise had to be constrained.
Trade was the initial battleground. The administration invoked Section 301 to investigate Chinese intellectual-property practices and forced technology transfer, followed by tariffs covering hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese imports. The January 2020 Phase One agreement subsequently sought to convert this confrontation into a negotiated bargain, securing Chinese commitments on purchases of American agricultural and energy products as well as intellectual-property protections.
But trade was only one component of a much broader strategy. The administration tightened technology restrictions, expanded measures against Chinese firms linked to the military, and increasingly scrutinised Chinese activity in Hong Kong and Xinjiang. Washington also adopted a more explicit position on Taiwan and South China Sea. Officials such as Matt Pottinger and Mike Pompeo helped articulate a more comprehensive critique of the Chinese political and economic model.
The apparent contradiction between Trump’s personal outreach to Xi and his escalating pressure on Beijing was therefore central rather than incidental. Personal diplomacy was used to manage a relationship that was simultaneously being redefined as competitive. The objective was no longer simply to induce China to become a more responsible participant in the existing order; it was to alter the terms on which the US and China interacted.
The second Trump administration initially appeared set to intensify this trajectory. During the campaign, Trump had threatened tariffs substantially higher than those imposed during his first term. In early 2025, the administration moved rapidly, combining new tariffs, fentanyl-related duties, restrictions affecting small-package imports and the broader reciprocal-tariff campaign. At their peak, tariffs on Chinese goods approached 145 per cent.
Beijing responded in kind, including through tariffs and restrictions involving critical rare-earth supplies.
The result was a rapid movement from escalation towards bargaining. Tariffs were reduced through successive truces, while some technology restrictions were eased. The administration also became less willing to allow disputes over Taiwan, South China Sea, human rights or China’s political system to obstruct commercial negotiations. The centre of gravity of China policy consequently shifted from comprehensive strategic confrontation towards managed economic competition.
The October 2025 Busan understanding was particularly significant in this respect. The emerging arrangement combined tariff reductions with Chinese commitments on agricultural purchases and a pause in some rare-earth restrictions. Subsequent negotiations, including Trump’s May visit to Beijing, further reinforced the emphasis on purchases, investment and institutionalised economic dialogue.
This did not amount to the abandonment of competition. Rather, competition was being placed within a more transactional framework. Technology controls, supply-chain diversification and concerns about China’s industrial power remained. But the administration increasingly appeared willing to moderate these instruments when doing so could produce a tangible commercial gain.
The September 2026 Xi-Trump summit in Washington provided the clearest illustration of this recalibration. Xi’s first state visit to Washington since 2015 was accompanied by considerable ceremony, with Trump personally greeting the Chinese leader and hosting a state dinner. Yet, the substantive outcomes were incremental.
The existing trade truce was extended to January 10, 2027, while the two sides agreed on preferential tariff treatment covering roughly $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction. Institutional mechanisms such as Boards of Trade and Investment were formalised, alongside an AI dialogue and an incident-communication channel. There was also agreement on continued summit-level engagement, including participation in forthcoming APEC and G20 meetings, while discussions continued on military crisis communications and missing-in-action remains cooperation.
These arrangements are useful for managing the relationship, but they do not resolve its central contradictions. There was no major breakthrough on technology self-reliance, the underlying trade imbalance, critical-mineral competition beyond the earlier pause, or the principal security disputes. Taiwan was raised by the Chinese side, particularly in relation to opposition to independence, but it featured far less prominently in the public American readout.
The summit therefore demonstrated the strengths and weaknesses of Trump’s personalised diplomacy. It can create political space for temporary bargains and reduce the immediate risk of escalation.
There is both continuity and change in Trump’s China policy.
The continuity is evident in the centrality of tariffs, the emphasis on reciprocity and trade deficits, and the preference for direct leader-to-leader bargaining. The instruments of economic coercion developed during the first term have not disappeared.
What has changed is the breadth of the strategic agenda. The first-term approach increasingly linked economic competition to technology, ideology, human rights, alliances and military strategy. The second-term approach has narrowed the immediate objective to economic advantage and managed coexistence. The language of an emerging “new Cold War” has consequently become less central to official policy, while the willingness to compromise on selected technology restrictions and avoid geopolitical flashpoints has increased.
This should not be mistaken for the disappearance of strategic competition. The underlying contest over technology, supply chains, industrial capacity and the military balance remains intact. What has changed is the hierarchy of priorities.
Trump’s second-term China policy is therefore best understood not as a return to engagement but as a more transactional form of competition. Washington continues to regard China as a major challenger, yet it is increasingly seeking to compartmentalise that rivalry and extract short-term economic gains without allowing every strategic disagreement to become a confrontation.
The September summit illustrated precisely this tension. The optics of personal diplomacy were strong, while the substantive gains remained limited. Washington obtained additional commercial commitments and political theatre; Beijing secured additional time and space for its economic and technological objectives. The larger structural contest, however, remains unresolved.
The evolution of Trump’s China policy thus reflects a change in the operating logic of the strategic competition: from a broad campaign to reshape the US-China relationship towards a more personalised, transactional effort to manage an increasingly unavoidable rivalry.

articles.title_orig: 2,000 arrested in France as student protests escalate into violence
articles.title_zh: 2,000 arrested in France as student protests escalate into violence
articles.content_orig:
PARIS  — About 400 schools in France are expected to remain ​closed on Friday after student protests over education-related grievances turned violent in some ‌places.
The protests against teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings erupted in the Paris region last month but have turned increasingly violent as they spread nationwide, with dozens injured and police making ​hundreds of arrests.
“There is an active and violent minority (participating in the protests) ... ​We’re not entirely sure that they are even high-school students themselves,” Justice ⁠Minister Gerald Darmanin told RTL radio on Friday, adding that 2,000 people had ​been arrested since the protests began, with about two-thirds placed in police custody.
“We have ​gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public-order disturbance. When people target buses and set schools on fire, it is no longer simply a protest issue”, he also said.
In an interview with ​broadcaster France 2, French Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Thursday evening that “a ​little over 400 schools and other educational establishments” would remain closed on Friday.
According to a source ‌close ⁠to Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, intelligence agencies told a crisis meeting on Thursday that the protest movement had been initiated by politicians from the hard left, including members of La France Insoumise (LFI).
LFI lawmaker Louis Boyard denied the claim in comments to ​French broadcasters.
Student protesters started ​fires in at ⁠least two high schools on Thursday, while teachers were inadvertently splashed with petrol at a third in the southern city of ​Marseille, officials said. At least one car was torched in ​Strasbourg in ⁠the east and riot police clashed with youths in Toulouse in the southwest.
Some high school students in the city of Liège in neighboring Belgium also began protesting on Thursday. ⁠According ​to local media, authorities in Liège announced that ​all schools in the city would close on Friday. A spokesperson for the municipality did not immediately confirm ​the closures.

articles.title_orig: Divers find body of person missing from California helicopter crash that killed 2 others
articles.title_zh: Divers find body of person missing from California helicopter crash that killed 2 others
articles.content_orig:
Death toll of medical helicopter crash is now three people as two others continue to recover from injuries, authorities say
Police divers have found the body of a patient who went missing after a medical helicopter crashed into the Pacific Ocean off Catalina Island near Los Angeles, bringing the death toll to three while two other people were recovering from their injuries, the authorities said on Friday.
Divers with the Los Angeles county sheriff’s department found the victim’s body Thursday in the wreckage of the helicopter after searching more than 156 sq miles (404 sq km) over 23 hours, the Coast Guard said in a statement.
Relatives of the missing person told local TV network ABC7 that the woman was being transported from Catalina Island to the mainland for medical care after having an allergic reaction. They also said her 20-year-old son went with her in the helicopter to help as a language interpreter.
The helicopter with five people onboard went down shortly after takeoff and hit the water not far from the island, officials said. The cause is not clear and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating. First responders pulled four people from the water on Wednesday night.
Robert Luna, the Los Angeles county sheriff, said authorities were not yet identifying the victims by name. But he described two of the people who died as the male pilot and a female nurse. He also said another medic and a fourth person, a man, were hospitalized. Luna said the helicopter wreckage was about 200ft (60m) deep in the water.
The helicopter’s operator, Reach Air Medical Services of Sacramento, confirmed that two of its crew members died and a third was recovering at a hospital. The company declined to provide more details.
A memorial service was held on the island to honor the victims.
The helicopter had landed on the island shortly after 7pm after a 24-minute flight from an airport in Oceanside, on the California coast between Los Angeles and San Diego, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24.
Janice Hahn, the Los Angeles county supervisor, said it was a terrible tragedy, adding: “The people who were on board dedicated their careers to saving lives. They are heroes.”

articles.title_orig: Nutrition study highlights performance benefit of sodium bicarbonate and carbohydrate co-ingestion
articles.title_zh: Nutrition study highlights performance benefit of sodium bicarbonate and carbohydrate co-ingestion
articles.content_orig:
Runners in action ( © World Athletics Dan Vernon )
The co-ingestion of sodium bicarbonate and carbohydrate could help athletes sustain high-intensity efforts later in a race while fatigued, according to a new study conducted by Bernardo R. Norte at the Research Institute for Sport and Exercise Sciences (RISES), Liverpool John Moores University, in collaboration with the World Athletics Health and Science Department.
In sport, the smallest detail can make the difference between victory and defeat. Winning a race can depend on the ability to deliver another intense effort when the body is already exhausted. With this in mind, the research led by Norte, a PhD student in exercise metabolism & nutrition, examined a novel energy gel combining sodium bicarbonate and carbohydrate during three hours of moderate-intensity exercise, followed by a series of high-intensity efforts, to assess performance in a fatigued state. It found that compared with carbohydrate ingestion alone, adding sodium bicarbonate improved performance after prolonged exercise and induced only mild gastrointestinal discomfort.
Research at the Research Institute for Sport and Exercise Sciences (RISES), Liverpool John Moores University
“A central finding of this study is that this new energy gel format may offer endurance athletes a practical nutritional strategy to achieve blood alkalosis and improve performance,” said Dr. Julien B. Louis, Reader in Nutrition and Exercise Physiology and the supervisor of the project.
Indeed, high-intensity exercise can temporarily cause metabolic acidosis, characterised by increased hydrogen-ion concentration and a reduction in blood pH. Fingertip blood samples were collected and analysed at regular intervals using a blood gas analyser (EPOC, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany). The results indicated that sodium bicarbonate ingestion during exercise helped limit acidosis thanks to its buffering capacity.
These findings suggest that the ergogenic potential of sodium bicarbonate may extend beyond isolated high-intensity exercise performed in a rested state and offer practical guidance for coaches and athletes, supporting more informed decision-making in both training and competition.
Researchers from the Research Institute for Sport and Exercise Sciences (RISES), Liverpool John Moores University
The full article is available for download from the Health & Science section of the World Athletics Library , under ‘nutrition in athletics’.

articles.title_orig: How Trump’s obsession with ‘rigged’ voting machines spread across US government
articles.title_zh: How Trump’s obsession with ‘rigged’ voting machines spread across US government
articles.content_orig:
A technical review that began with one voting machine soon drew several federal agencies—and raised fresh fears about who could seize election records.
In June 2025, a team of U.S. government computer specialists traveled between a warehouse in Puerto Rico and the headquarters of the island’s election commission. They examined a voting machine used in the 2024 election, looking for evidence that could cast doubt on the established account of the 2020 U.S. presidential election.
The operation was led by Kurt Olsen, a Washington lawyer who had spent years promoting Donald Trump’s false claims of election fraud. Trump and his supporters insisted that foreign powers might have changed the results in Joe Biden’s favor. Courts, audits, election officials and intelligence agencies repeatedly rejected those allegations.
The examination of a single machine later grew into an investigation involving the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security and the FBI. According to people familiar with Olsen’s work, the investigation had two goals: to find evidence of fraud in the 2020 election and use it to justify sweeping changes to the U.S. election system.
Some White House and intelligence officials believed that evidence of interference by foreign powers or Trump’s political opponents could provide grounds for expanding federal authority over elections. Election officials fear that this work laid the groundwork for federal agents to potentially seize voting equipment or ballots during the midterm elections in November.
The White House said the investigation was initiated by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, then led by Tulsi Gabbard. It said the inquiry was prompted by concerns raised by Puerto Rico election officials and relayed through the U.S. attorney’s office, and that its purpose was to identify vulnerabilities, not revisit the 2020 election. But according to people familiar with the investigation, Olsen pushed to find evidence of foreign interference. The inquiry later expanded to Georgia and Arizona and involved several federal agencies.
The White House also denied that its career staff were involved in the decision to obtain and examine the machine in Puerto Rico. But Olsen, who had Trump’s backing, was in regular contact with administration officials before the operation began. One person familiar with the matter said the White House and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence coordinated before the equipment was brought from the island. Later, as the investigation expanded beyond Puerto Rico, senior White House officials became involved.
The Office of the Director of National Intelligence, Gabbard, the CIA, the Department of Homeland Security and the Justice Department did not respond to requests for comment. The U.S. attorney’s office in Puerto Rico declined to comment.
The investigation found no evidence that foreign powers had infiltrated U.S. election systems, tampered with machines or affected the outcome of the 2020 election. According to three people familiar with the matter, Olsen told colleagues that intelligence agencies and White House officials were obstructing the work by withholding information he needed.
Election officials fear that voting machines will once again become targets of disinformation and fraud allegations ahead of the midterm elections. Some are preparing legal documents and making contingency plans in case federal agents demand that they hand over equipment or records. In June, Colorado passed a law allowing the state to declare an election emergency in the event of federal interference, including attempts to obtain voting equipment or documents. Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat, said the state would be ready to respond.
Ben Berwick, head of the election law and litigation team at the organization Protect Democracy, said the campaign by Olsen and his allies undermines trust in elections and could create conditions for future interference. Meanwhile, Trump supporters who had spent years promoting conspiracy theories about voting machines had gained influence in the federal government.
By the start of Trump’s second term, Olsen was already known among activists who claimed that the 2020 election had been stolen. He represented Kari Lake, a former Arizona gubernatorial candidate backed by Trump, in a case over her defeat in the 2022 election. A state court fined Olsen $2,000 for falsely claiming that tens of thousands of illegal votes had been included in the count. At a disciplinary hearing over his license to practice in Arizona, he said he had learned his lesson and would choose his words more carefully going forward.
Olsen also worked closely with Mike Lindell, founder of MyPillow, who spread false claims that voting machines had changed votes in 2020. Trump, who retained Olsen as his lawyer after the election, introduced the two in February 2021. Lindell called Olsen his partner in matters of election fraud.
One theory they promoted was that code belonging to Smartmatic, a company founded by people from Venezuela, had made its way into Dominion equipment. This supposedly could have allowed the government of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to manipulate votes. Courts repeatedly rejected these claims for lack of evidence, and both companies denied them.
Smartmatic spokesperson Samira Saba said that years of reviews, investigations, lawsuits and technical examinations had uncovered no credible evidence that the company’s software code had been used to change votes in 2020. Liberty Vote, which acquired Dominion in 2025, declined to answer questions about Olsen’s investigation but said it was focused on reliability, service and transparency.
After Trump returned to power, Olsen argued to White House and intelligence officials that evidence of foreign interference could justify expanding federal authority over elections. The U.S. Constitution leaves election oversight primarily to the states. At the same time, the administration was preparing an executive order, which Trump signed in March, requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote and proposing restrictions on certain methods of voting by mail.
In spring 2025, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence created a group called the Director’s Initiative Group to carry out Trump’s executive orders targeting what he and his allies called the politicization of government and intelligence agencies. The group’s first project was an investigation into the 2020 election. It was led by a senior intelligence official, retired Army Lt. Col. Paul McNamara.
McNamara brought in Mohave Research, which had helped the Office of the Director of National Intelligence develop internal search tools. According to two former officials, the White House asked the office to work with Olsen on election projects. It was not possible to establish exactly how Olsen, who did not then hold a government position, came to play a central role. McNamara also invited Jason Weagham, head of Mohave Research. Weagham said he was brought in to examine machines in Puerto Rico alongside Olsen.
Puerto Rico gave Olsen and his allies access to Dominion machines similar to those used in the United States. Local officials agreed to the examination after problems with ballot scanners, including jams and errors reading votes, disrupted the 2024 election.
According to people familiar with the investigation, Olsen spoke with White House officials almost daily and assembled a small team of outside analysts. He shared election-related information with them that he obtained from government agencies. The White House said the administration complies with laws governing access to sensitive information.

articles.title_orig: Top Democrats slam ‘Trump’s failing economic agenda’ after weaker-than-expected jobs growth – US politics live
articles.title_zh: Top Democrats slam ‘Trump’s failing economic agenda’ after weaker-than-expected jobs growth – US politics live
articles.content_orig:
Elizabeth Warren and Chuck Schumer criticize president after US added 29,000 new jobs in September, sharply less than the 84,000 economists had predicted
Sign up for the Breaking News US email
Send us your questions on how the Iran war will affect US voters in the midterms
Elizabeth Warren , the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, has blasted Donald Trump’s “failing economic agenda” following the latest jobs report – which many experts have described as “mediocre” and “weak”.
“Since January 2025, Trump’s economy has only added 33,000 jobs a month on average, far below the 120,000-a-month average in 2024,” Warren said. “Since the start of Trump’s war, real wages have fallen 0.7% as his failed agenda keeps pushing prices up.”
Ahead of the November midterms, Democrats are hammering home that many of the Trump administration’s policies have resulted in a cost of living crisis, and urging voters to eschew Republicans vying for seats in Congress at the ballot box.
Meanwhile, Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, noted that “American families are being squeezed on all sides by Trump’s disastrous economy”, in response to Friday’s figures.
A group of environmental organizations have sued the Trump administration over its recent move to slash clean-car rules that had been aimed at reducing planet-heating emissions and boosting electric vehicles.
On Monday, the administration relaxed the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (Cafe) standards that regulate how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline.
Donald Trump said last week that the less stringent mileage requirements would “take the waste out of building cars in America” and save families “thousands on a new, beautiful and safe car”, while boosting auto production in the US.
Trump has repeatedly pledged to end what he falsely calls an EV “mandate”, referring incorrectly to Joe Biden’s target that half of all new vehicle sales be electric by 2030. No federal policy has mandated auto companies to sell EVs.
Sean Duffy , the US transportation secretary, hailed the new initiative – called Freedom Means Affordable Cars – which the agency said would reduce the average cost of new vehicles by $1,300, and save consumers $138bn over the next five years.
The lawsuit is currently a petition to review the Department of Transportation’s move.
Ahead of Donald Trump heading to Mobile, Alabama today, it’s worth pointing out a new poll from AP-Norc which shows that a majority of Americans blame the president for their struggle with the cost of living .
This also comes as the latest jobs report shows tepid growth and a rise in unemployment. What’s more, wage growth has not kept up with inflation.
More than 60% of respondents say that the economy is worse off since Trump took office , and 52% of Republicans surveyed say that the president’s handling of the cost of living has been worse than expected .
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) – which serves as the official campaign arm for House Democrats – moved eight districts on their map of targets this midterm cycle to “in play” .
Their list now includes, Virginia’s sixth, Washington state’s fifth, North Carolina’s 13th, Kansas’ second, Texas’ ninth, Oklahoma’s fifth, New Jersey’s second and Michigan’s first . This means the DCCC has identified 66 critical districts as competitive, in order for Democrats to reclaim control of the lower chamber.
While some forecasters expect the party to win the House, many of the competitions are neck-and-neck. The last time Democrats saw a so-called “blue wave” was in 2018 – when they flipped 41 seats.
The top Republican aligned Super Pac, the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), will pause it’s multimillion dollar ad spend in North Carolina in support of Michael Whatley , the GOP nominee for the open US Senate seat, according to multiple reports.
Democrats are hoping to flip the Tar Heel state in the upcoming midterm elections, where they need to net four seats in order to reclaim control of the Senate. Roy Cooper , North Carolina’s former governor, is the Democratic nominee and is leading Whatley in every poll, in some cases by double digits.
The SLF initially announced a $71m investment in the North Carolina race back in April – noting that Whatley – the former chair of the Republican National Committee with backing from Donald Trump – was a “battle-tested leader”. Semafor first reported the news that SLF shifting its spending priority, and is now reserving a seven-figure sum for the Senate race in Kansas – which has become increasingly competitive as Trump’s approval rating hits a record low nationwide.
While a Democrat hasn’t won a Senate seat in the Sunflower state in almost a century , the race between Republican incumbent Roger Marshall and his Democratic challenger, pastor Adam Hamilton , has become more of a concern for the GOP. The Cook Political Report, a prominent election forecaster, downgraded the competition from “leans Republican” to “likely Republican” at the end of September.
Democratic ⁠senators said today that they expect a ⁠vote before 13 ⁠December ​on the Trump administration’s pact ⁠to share nuclear power technology with Saudi Arabia .
“ The ⁠Senate will now ​have a ‌chance ‌to fulfill its statutory responsibility ‌to study and weigh in on the impact this agreement could have in driving a ‌nuclear arms race in the Middle East ​and potentially undermining nuclear nonproliferation efforts around the world ,” senator Jeff ⁠Merkley said in ​a ​release reported ​first by Reuters.
Merkley ​worked ‌on getting ​the ​vote with four of his fellow Democrats.
The US will deploy about 500 troops to Texas’s Rio Grande valley this week, days after Coast Guard personnel came under fire from suspected cartel members near the Mexican border, NewsNation reports citing law enforcement sources.
NewsNation reported it had obtained video showing troops being dropped on to islands in the sector from Chinook helicopters.
The Coast Guard said Coast Guard Forces Rio Grande personnel encountered gunfire from the Mexican border near Garceno, Texas, on Saturday while conducting joint interdiction operations with federal partners, according to NewsNation’s report. Personnel returned fire in the incident, which is still under investigation.
No injuries to Coast Guard or other personnel were reported, and no damage to Coast Guard assets was reported.
Chris Stein , Alex Clark , Andrew Witherspoon and Ashley Kirk
A turning point in Donald Trump ’s second term will soon arrive. On 3 November, voters across the US will decide whether to keep the president’s Republican allies in control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority.
Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of the House of Representatives , and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration.
This interactive piece charts and maps reveal where the battle for Congress will be fought.
This year’s Kennedy Center Honors will be held at Washington’s Capital One Arena, not the arts institution that’s been at the center of a legal battle over adding Donald Trump ’s name to the building, the Associated Press reports.
The 49th annual awards are set to take place at Washington’s downtown arena, a Kennedy Center spokesperson said. Few other details were immediately available, and an explanation for the change wasn’t given. The event will take place on 7 December.
The center’s Trump-picked board voted last month to close the performing arts venue after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump’s name to the facade.
Trump has threatened in social media posts that safety repairs the center needs would only happen if the board was allowed to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.

articles.title_orig: How to time your flu shot and pick the best option
articles.title_zh: How to time your flu shot and pick the best option
articles.content_orig:
There’s a bit of a chill in the air, pumpkin spice in your coffee and children back to school — which means the threat of respiratory viruses like Covid-19, influenza and RSV is looming.
Some respiratory illnesses have arrived already. Seasonal influenza activity is still low at the national level, data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows.
But certain flu metrics are inching up – especially in the West . Health officials in Washington state’s King County note that since mid-August there has been an increase in people with flu visiting emergency departments in the area.
Related video above | When is the best time to get your flu shot?
Vaccines that help prevent illness and reduce the risk of serious infections and hospitalization are now available, and for some people, this is the right time to roll up their sleeves.
Typically, the CDC launches a fall campaign around this time of year, recommending seasonal immunizations such as the flu shot and Covid-19 vaccines. But after sweeping changes to the agency’s vaccine advisory committee during the second Trump administration and ongoing lawsuits, the CDC recently posted guidance online to follow last year’s recommendations for flu and Covid-19.
Meanwhile, the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project launched their own independent reviews of this fall’s vaccines – including those for flu , Covid and RSV – which were published in September in the medical journal JAMA.
The review papers helped inform 2026-27 respiratory virus immunization recommendations released by several medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.
“For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP,” Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a news briefing.
“Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter,” Gellin said.
“Clinicians will still have patients to care for. Parents will still have decisions to make for their children, and older Americans, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions will still need to know how best to protect themselves,” he said. “We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance.”
The US Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN’s request for comment on the groups’ recommendations.
Flu, Covid-19 and RSV immunizations are now available at most major pharmacies.
“And really reassuringly, insurers have indicated to the major groups that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations,” Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in a news briefing.
Ordering through Vaccines for Children, the federal program that provides routine immunizations at no cost to children who are uninsured or underinsured or whose families may not otherwise be able to afford them, has also started. About half of US children are eligible for the program.
“Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives,” Nosal said in a news release. “As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients.”
The groups eligible for RSV immunizations include older adults, pregnant people and infants.
“People age 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75 years old, should get one dose,” Nosal said. “This is not an annual vaccine. If you got one before, you do not need a new one this year. Getting one should protect you throughout the entire season.”
During pregnancy, RSV vaccination is recommended in the third trimester, between weeks 32 and 36.
Children younger than 8 months should be immunized against RSV using a monoclonal antibody unless their mother got an RSV vaccination during pregnancy, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.
“If the mother’s immunization status is unknown, that child should be immunized,” Racine said in the briefing. He added that children between 8 months and 19 months of age who are in certain high-risk groups for severe disease are also recommended to get the RSV monoclonal antibody.
And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems.
“Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for severe disease than immunocompetent individuals,” Dr. Dan Barouch, director of the Center for Virology and Vaccine Research at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, who was not involved in the new recommendations, said in an email. “The vaccines are also generally less effective in immunosuppressed individuals compared with immunocompetent individuals.”
For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall.
The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people.
“ACOG now recommends that pregnant individuals receive a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, from September 1 through March 1 instead of only through January 31,” Dr. Christina Davidson, chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said in the news briefing.
“We made this change because the RSV disease season is now occurring later in the spring, and it is also more severe than it used to be,” Davidson said. “The extension of the eligibility window will help provide pregnant patients and their infants with additional protection.”
For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March.
Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot.
“On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%,” Nosal said.
“Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it’s available,” she said. “But do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available.”
And for the first time, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for use in adults 50 and older.
The flu vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy, but pregnant people should avoid the nasal spray version, according to the recommendations.
“Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people,” Davidson said.
“The inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccines remain the only vaccines that are recommended for use in pregnancy in any trimester, so please work with your OB care clinician or pharmacist to get these,” she said. “Most importantly, if you are able to get the vaccine while you are pregnant, the immunity will also, in part, pass on to your baby.”
October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because “protection wanes throughout the season.”
Some providers use the slogan “ flu before boo ” to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween.
Getting an updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for adults.
“If you’re older than 19, we recommend getting the Covid-19 vaccine,” Nosal said.

articles.title_orig: US and China release $60 billion nonsensitive product lists for tariff cuts after Trump-Xi meeting
articles.title_zh: US and China release $60 billion nonsensitive product lists for tariff cuts after Trump-Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG (AP) — The United States and China on Monday released reciprocal lists of nonsensitive products worth about $30 billion each that will see tariff cuts, from American hair products to Chinese toys, in a deal expected to help bolster bilateral trade.
The details came days after Chinese President Xi Jinping met with U.S. President Donald Trump in Washington in his first state visit to the U.S. since 2015. The U.S. had already reduced tariffs against China after Trump’s tariffs reached as high as 145% at one point last year, as tensions between the two countries eased.

articles.title_orig: Nike shares plummet 10% after weak revenue outlook and layoff plans underway
articles.title_zh: Nike shares plummet 10% after weak revenue outlook and layoff plans underway
articles.content_orig:
Nike's shares plummeted in premarket trading Friday, falling for a second straight day after it reported falling revenue and plans to lay off staff in 2027.
The sportswear giant said Thursday that its fiscal first-quarter revenues were down 4% to $11.2 billion, citing declines in Greater China, which was partially offset by growth in its North America segment. Its net income was  $712 million, down 2% from $727 million the previous year.
"We have more work to do in NIKE Sportswear, Jordan Brand and Greater China, and we're taking deliberate actions to strengthen those businesses the right way for the long term," Nike President and CEO Elliott Hill said in the release.
Nike expects revenues to decline in the high-single digits in 2027. Its shares were last down 10.36% in premarket trading on Friday and have declined nearly 45% since the beginning of the year.
The company also announced its new operating model "Pace," which is expected to deliver $2.5 billion in cost savings by 2031, with plans to lay off more staff starting in 2027.
"This work will result in fewer roles across Nike, and I want to acknowledge that news like this creates uncertainty. I don't take that lightly," Hill said in a separate announcement on Thursday. "Decisions about impacted roles related to this work will begin in calendar year 2027 and beyond."
The program also includes efforts to modernize Nike's global supply chain, organizing into three geographies, establishing a new campus in India, and further streamlining the organization to reduce costs.
Nike has already carried out layoffs twice since the beginning of the year, including cutting 775 jobs across its U.S. distribution centers in January, and letting go of a further 1,400 employees primarily in its tech division in April.
Citi analysts said in a note Friday that they will remain "neutral" on the company as its sales guidance came in below market expectations.
"Nike is turning into a cost-cutting story, announcing a $2.5bn cost savings program as management is adapting to the reality of significant pressure within Sportswear, Jordan, and China," the Citi analysts said.
They noted that management will offer more detail on its five-year outlook at their investor day, but details around when Pace will actually "move the dial" will only come in 2029.
"It isn't out of the question that Nike can beat some of the guidance they just provided, but there really is no justification (in our view) for Nike to receive a premium multiple versus its growing peers," they added.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures rise ahead of key jobs report as oil steadies
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures rise ahead of key jobs report as oil steadies
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices were sharply lower on Friday morning, extending losses from earlier in the session, following reports of a potential move to release diesel and crude stocks to ease a global supply shortage.
International benchmark Brent crude futures with December expiry traded 3.1% lower at $99.13 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with November expiry fell 4% to $89.18.
It comes shortly after Reuters reported that European Union member states were discussing a French proposal to release additional diesel reserves following pressure from the Trump administration .
The report, which cited a single unnamed source familiar with details of the discussion, said France had proposed that EU nations release 50 million barrels of diesel and International Energy Agency members release 50 million barrels of crude oil.
CNBC could not independently verify the report. A spokesperson for the French government and the IEA were not immediately available to comment.
The EU is holding crisis talks on Friday to discuss a coordinated response to soaring diesel prices after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on European countries to urgently release some of the continent's reserves.
In a post on social media, Bessent said Thursday that aAmerica's European partners "should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions."
He added: "American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage."
U.S. President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly touted the prospect of a diesel export ban, appeared to cool on the idea earlier this week, following a resurgence in crude exports through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.
The U.S. supplied around half of the EU's diesel imports in August, according to the International Energy Agency, underscoring the 27-nation bloc's exposure to a potential export ban.
Oil prices settled higher in the previous session amid a report that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, along with an amphibious force carrying 2,000 Marines, raising the stakes for an escalation in the months-long conflict.
